articles.title: Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Existing work suggests that markets can show volatility with paths rougher than those of Brownian motion. In theory this can happen when the order flow is close to instability with memory that decays as a power law. However, it is not fully clear how such order flow could arise from the predominantly algorithmic market making that characterizes order book dynamics. We show one such consistent mechanism. We treat each market maker as a desk that uses a first-order gradient rule to move the distances of its orders from the mid price toward target distances provided by an unknown oracle. We assume that distinct desks do not act synchronously in time but act whenever new information relevant to their respective oracles arrives, which each desk samples over its own characteristic lookback horizon. Across all desks the rule therefore takes the form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with information-driven (mini-batch) noise. In the continuum limit this update rule makes the volume of the order book follow a conservative stochastic partial differential equation (the Dean--Kawasaki equation) whose fluctuations drive the order flow. The distinct horizons of the desks further induce a persistent memory in the order flow that decays as a power law. Standard scaling arguments then lead to rough volatility. We confirm the key predictions of the model on simulated agents and on six months of Binance data with about 790 million orders. In liquid markets governed mainly by market makers, such as the perpetual futures of Binance, the order books are consistent with how our desks change the book.

articles.title: Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.

articles.title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

articles.title: Who Should Be on the Panel? Task-Conditioned Persona Selection for LLM Trading Agents
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: Multi-agent LLM systems are built by fixing a cast of roles and then designing how the cast coordinates. Which agents should make up the group for a given task is left to the designer, and the same cast is reused for every task. Financial trading makes the cost of that choice visible: stocks trade differently, and the trading styles suited to one need not suit another. We study task-conditioned persona selection, composing the group from the characteristics of the task it will face, and instantiate it with FinPanel, an LLM multi-agent trading system in which a recruiter selects a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how the stock trades, each persona gives an independent daily call in its own style, and a manager commits the trade after reading the panel's arguments and their desk-kept, hierarchical track records. Because nothing is returned to the traders, the panel stays the panel that was selected, and it can trade a new stock from an empty record. On eight US stocks over the out-of-knowledge year 2025, against three prior LLM trading agents re-implemented in the same framework and against rule-based, predictive and reinforcement-learning baselines, the selected panel is ahead of a fixed panel of the same size and of the prior agents run as their papers prescribe, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock; it keeps its performance with no warm-up and with no record at all, whereas the memory-augmented agents' returns swing with their warm-up; and neither more seats nor the manager's reading of the arguments substitutes for selecting the right ones. Who is in the group is a design decision to be made per task, before how the group coordinates.

articles.title: How To Build Financial AI Capacity As A Competitive Advantage
articles.query: site:forbes.com "machine learning" (bank OR banking OR fintech OR lending OR fraud OR credit)
articles.text:
Dr. Ravi Gedela, CEO, Banking Labs Inc. , an AI-powered financial intelligence company.
The global financial system stands at the threshold of a fundamental structural realignment driven by artificial intelligence (AI). It is a paradigm shift at its macro scale, intensified by the fast-paced penetration into vertical domains of global finance and, notably, capital markets, regulatory compliance and financial crime risk management.​
For leaders across large banks, institutional investment firms and payment service providers, navigating this shift is no longer a discretionary IT modernization effort. It is an existential imperative for long-term business growth and market leadership.
However, critical questions remain: Is AI a hyperscale trap of cash flow or a real business growth opportunity? Why do many AI programs stall in large institutions? And what must change for them to succeed?
Over the next decade, financial institutions will experience a dramatic reallocation of enterprise value. Historically, much of a firm’s value has resided in human capital: the knowledge, execution capability and client networks of senior bankers and deal teams. In the emerging operational model, that value anchor migrates to proprietary software architectures, governed data assets and institutional context layers that the firm owns.
Achieving this transition requires leadership to systematically extract the latent domain expertise, tactical judgment and deal-making frameworks locked within the minds of their top human performers and permanently embed them into software assets. By transforming ephemeral human capability into compounding firm-wide intelligence infrastructure, institutions can ensure that their competitive moat expands continuously rather than walking out the door at the close of every business day.
​A common reason AI programs stall is that they often rely exclusively on generalist frontier model providers to run complex financial operations. Frontier labs produce exceptional raw cognitive engines, but they often optimize for horizontal, mass-market scale. Treasury, capital markets and financial crime risk management, by contrast, are specialized, confidential domains governed by strict regulatory mandates, distinct data topologies and exacting precision standards.
Generalist providers are unlikely to build the last-mile intelligence pipelines that finance requires: transaction venues that comply with jurisdiction-specific rules, material non-public information (MNPI) isolation barriers and deep integrations with systems of record, such as Bloomberg or Salesforce. That work would distract from hyperscale revenue targets and add regulatory exposure.
Sustainable value, therefore, requires purpose-built financial AI: architectures that wrap foundation models in operational harnesses, compliance guardrails and domain-specific integration layers. At Banking Labs, where my team builds financial AI across capital markets, compliance and financial crime, we have consistently found that this harness, not the model itself, is where durable advantage is won.
In private markets—where workflows historically suffered from manual human coordination, fragmented data and non-standardized documentation—vertical AI architectures can systematically execute core operational processes:
1. Data Room Preparation And Tearing: Agents can autonomously ingest, organize, cross-examine and extract key metrics from incoming virtual data room documents, cross-referencing company performance against firm-specific investment mandates.
2. Confidential Information Memorandum (CIM) Drafting: The system can synthesize internal financial models, market positioning data and competitive landscapes into comprehensive, publication-ready deal decks and investment committee memos.
3. Buyer Outreach And DDQ Processing: AI can facilitate the autonomous coordination of targeted buyer lists, tailored outreach tracking and the automated intake, resolution and verification of complex due diligence questionnaires (DDQs).
4. Executive Markup Workflows: These systems can help modernize senior leadership interfaces by enabling executives to mark up presentations directly on mobile devices or via email. The AI harness can parse these handwritten or text markups, execute structural edits across underlying files and return fully revised presentation decks within, in my experience, 20 minutes (down from a standard two-day turnaround using junior staff). Simultaneously, the engine can generate complete, transparent audit trails detailing every modification for junior bankers to inspect and verify.
While private markets require the constant navigation of unstructured data, public markets can present structured, data-rich environments ideal for advanced multiagent architectures. In these venues, firms can deploy sophisticated agentic frameworks, such as multiagent debate clusters. While automated execution can dramatically accelerate transaction velocity, operating at scale requires rigorous compliance architectures to ensure speed never compromises legal defensibility.​
Model risk management is being reshaped in both the United States and Canada. In April 2026, U.S. banking regulators replaced SR 11-7, the guidance that had governed model risk for 15 years, with SR 26-2 . The new framework is more principles-based, and regulators have indicated that AI-specific expectations will follow.
Canada is moving in the same direction. OSFI’s revised Guideline E-23, effective May 1, 2027, brings AI and machine learning models explicitly within its scope. Its approach is proportional: Models with greater autonomy or customer impact require closer review and monitoring.
Institutions operating in both countries must therefore satisfy two regimes on different timelines. Both, however, require AI that is governed, explainable and auditable. General-purpose models struggle to meet this standard on their own. Vertical financial AI, designed with lineage and controls from the outset, is better positioned to do so.
In institutional compliance, lineage auditability outranks raw statistical accuracy. A highly accurate model that operates as a black box cannot withstand a regulatory examination or judicial discovery. In the agentic era, explaining a single model is not enough; institutions must be able to prove, step-by-step, how every AI-assisted decision was made.
This answers the questions I began with. AI can become a cash trap when institutions treat it as a technology function delegated to large vendors offering frontier models. It becomes a growth engine when they invest in domain-specific, vertical AI capacity that they own and govern. Large institutions should pivot from the convenience of outsourcing AI to the discipline of building AI capital.
Before the next budget cycle, executives should ask one question: If a regulator asked tomorrow why our AI made a specific decision, could we show them, step-by-step, how it came to that decision?​​

articles.title: How Banks Can Govern Customer-Owned AI Agents They Don’t Own
articles.query: site:forbes.com ("generative AI" OR ChatGPT OR LLM) (finance OR bank OR investment OR insurance OR trading)
articles.text:
Alfred Kahn is the founder and CEO at OvationCXM , a customer experience management company.
​Most discussions about AI agents in banking focus on internal use cases. But clients are launching their own AI agents to automate finance and banking workflows. These agents are quickly becoming a new banking channel, so banks must prepare to govern them.
In our survey of 520 U.S. finance leaders , 75% said they are using or piloting AI agents in their workflows. Only 1 in 10 has no plans to use them.
In September, six banks, including Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Bank of America and Capital One, published voluntary principles for agentic commerce . They called for visibility into agent activity and customer control over delegated authority and execution. Standards are also being discussed, including the Personal Agent Protocol (Poppy), an open standard for how personal AI agents interact with businesses.
But principles and standards alone won’t operationalize agent governance. That requires infrastructure.
Customer agents come from many platforms. In our research, we found that finance leaders most often named AI tools like ChatGPT (39%) and Microsoft Copilot (36%), spreadsheets (32%), accounting suites (25%) and collaboration tools (22%). Few named bank portals (13%) or bank APIs (12%), likely because most banks lack a front door for machine interactions.
Bank controls were built for two types of users: a person logging into a portal, with entitlements, limits and a second approver, or a system connection, like a host-to-host file or API call running a preapproved process.
An AI agent is neither. It is not a named user, but it makes its own decisions. It looks like a system connection, but acts with human authority. Banks’ identity and authorization models aren’t designed to grant authority, limit it or capture what the agent did with it.
More APIs won’t fill the gap. APIs authenticate credentials, but they don’t validate whether the client gave its agent authority for that specific request. Closing the gap requires a checkpoint between the request and core banking systems that verifies the agent and the client it acts for, then applies the permissions end to end.
In our survey, 74% of respondents said agents will be important to their operations within a year. Those using, piloting or planning to use agents expect to use them within 12 months for at least one read-only banking task (77%), instruction task (71%) or money-movement task (68%).
Among finance leaders using agents, 54% said they would find an internal or third-party workaround if their bank couldn’t support agentic banking. That’s a real risk. Banks prioritize deposit retention and primacy in client relationships, and every workaround threatens both. The bank may own the account on paper and clear the payment, but the workflows migrate to platforms it doesn’t control.
Although the data shows rapid adoption of AI agents, finance leaders still want human oversight. Across eight banking tasks surveyed, leaders are almost as willing to allow money movement (50%) as read-only tasks (54%).
Willingness drops when humans are not in the loop: Only 10% would allow autonomous money movement and 17% would permit balance inquiries. Specific controls increase their confidence: Role-based permissions and transaction limits were chosen by 39%, and 38% want the ability to revoke agent access instantly.
Banks don’t control customer-owned agents, but they are responsible when those agents interact with bank systems.
1. Separate discovery from authorization. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a common standard for exposing tools to AI models, and banks should support it. But MCP is a menu. It tells an agent which functions exist and how to call them; it doesn’t decide whether the agent is allowed to call them for this client in this amount. That decision belongs outside the AI model, in a control plane that checks every request against the client’s entitlements, limits and approvals, as well as the bank’s own policies. A prompt can tell an agent not to transfer more than $10,000, but only a hard limit in the bank’s systems ensures it doesn’t.
2. Publish bounded tasks, not open APIs. Exposing raw REST endpoints gives AI agents too much reach into internal systems. Instead, expose discrete business actions, such as verifying payment status, fetching exception details or creating a service request. Scope each task by caller identity, target account, input parameters, transaction caps and approval policies. Read and write access must remain separate. A balance inquiry and a wire transfer should never share credentials.
3. Know the agent before you trust it. Vet every agent request with three tests. First, identify the agent, the provider and which client it belongs to. Then decide whether it’s a known agent on the account or a new one. Finally, confirm the client has delegated authority for this task, account and amount. Register each agent with its own credentials, tied to a client and limited to a subset of that client’s permissions. It should never log in as the client, and the bank should be able to revoke access in seconds for one agent, one client or an entire platform.
4. Stage rollout by risk. Start with read-only workflows you can check against bank records, such as transaction status. Confirm that policy blocks work as designed. Keep money movement behind treasury limits, dual approvals and mandatory human sign-offs until controls are validated.
Agents won’t erode bank relationships overnight; they’ll do it workflow by workflow as work moves outside the bank. Clients will use AI agents with or without their bank’s permission. The question is whether banks can keep control through their front door or clients build a back door around them—or they take their business elsewhere. Among finance leaders using agents, 15% of those we surveyed admitted they would move more of their banking if their institution couldn’t support AI ǐagents.
Agent governance is not just an AI strategy. It’s a retention and growth strategy.​​

articles.title: AI Agents Are Forcing Banks To Build A New Kind Of Finance Team
articles.query: site:forbes.com ("generative AI" OR ChatGPT OR LLM) (finance OR bank OR investment OR insurance OR trading)
articles.text:
Banks are creating a new finance function called AI FinOps to control the soaring costs of autonomous software agents. McKinsey reports that spending on the tokens powering these agents could reach 20% of banks’ labor costs. Elon Musk similarly acknowledged that running Grok Bot became unsustainably expensive relative to revenue. Unlike traditional software that sells access via subscriptions, AI agents sell work, consuming unpredictable computing resources through multiple reasoning steps. Gartner calls this the Inference Paradox, where cheaper AI models do not necessarily lower total costs because sophisticated workflows consume more computation. Consequently, companies like Salesforce are experimenting with different pricing models, including per-user fees, per-conversation charges, and per-action rates.
It sounds like an employer’s dream: employees who don’t ask for salaries, take vacations, or complain about their managers. They work around the clock, never call in sick, and can theoretically replace entire teams. But then the bill arrives.
This week, Reuters reported that banks are creating an entirely new finance function to manage their digital employees. They’re calling it AI FinOps, and its job is to keep the cost of autonomous software under control. According to McKinsey, spending on the tokens powering AI agents could reach 20% of banks’ labor costs.
Meanwhile, Elon Musk has encountered the same problem from the consumer side. According to Fortune, Musk acknowledged that running Grok Bot had become unsustainably expensive relative to revenue. The company responded by restricting the computing resources available to the product, leaving subscribers hitting their usage limits sooner.
For an industry promising to replace expensive human labor with tireless digital workers, this is quite a plot twist. The new employees don’t collect paychecks, but they do have expense accounts. And apparently, somebody needs to supervise them.
The economics start making sense once you understand what separates an AI agent from a chatbot.
When you ask ChatGPT to summarize a document, it processes the request and returns an answer. But when you ask an autonomous agent to prepare a competitive analysis, it might retrieve dozens of documents, search the web, consult other models, compare findings, question its conclusions and repeat several steps before deciding it’s finished.
Every action consumes computing resources, and every additional reasoning step, failed attempt or consultation with another agent can add to the cost.
Imagine hiring an analyst who charges by the minute, but also bills you for every document they read, every colleague they consult and every time they change their mind. Now imagine allowing that analyst to hire other analysts without asking permission. The productivity could be extraordinary, but so could the invoice.
This is exactly what banks are discovering: McKinsey’s Vik Sohoni explained to Reuters that traditional cost controls, such as directing simpler queries to cheaper models, become less effective when agents communicate with one another and rapidly consume tokens.
Hence AI FinOps: we spent decades automating financial operations. Now we’re building financial operations to supervise the automation.
Here’s where things become counterintuitive. AI inference, the computing required to generate responses, has been getting dramatically cheaper. One would assume that should make agents cheaper to operate, but as it turns out, not necessarily.
In August, Gartner predicted that providers’ inference costs per agentic workflow would increase more than fivefold by 2028. Importantly, that’s a forecast about what it costs providers to run these workflows, not a prediction that customers’ bills will increase fivefold.
Gartner calls this the Inference Paradox: Even as many AI models become cheaper to run, increasingly sophisticated agentic workflows consume more computation and often rely on more expensive models, pushing the total cost of completing a task higher.
Consider a hypothetical example: a task that once required 100 units of computation at one cent each costs a dollar. Now suppose computation becomes ten times cheaper, but a more capable agent uses twenty times as many units to complete a substantially more ambitious assignment. The provider’s computation cost has doubled.
Whether that’s good or bad economics depends on how much additional value the agent delivers, and how much the customer is willing to pay for it. That is the distinction that matters, and it cuts both ways: more expensive intelligence isn’t necessarily less profitable intelligence. But without a reliable connection between the cost of computation and the value of completed work, companies face a problem that traditional software vendors rarely encountered at this scale.
For decades, enterprise software companies sold access to tools, and the economics of that were great: predictable subscriptions, and little extra cost to serve one more customer.
AI agents increasingly sell work itself. And work is harder to price because its cost, complexity and value can vary enormously. Charge a fixed subscription, and heavy users may consume the vendor’s margins. Charge for every action, and customers face unpredictable bills. Charge for outcomes, and the vendor must decide how much computation to spend achieving them, while establishing what actually counts as success.
Salesforce is already experimenting with all three approaches. Its Agentforce pricing includes $125 per user per month for certain employee-facing products, $2 per customer conversation, or $0.10 per standard action. A simple customer inquiry might require only a few actions, while resolving a complicated issue could involve dozens. Salesforce is effectively offering three different answers to a question the software industry hasn’t yet settled: What exactly should we charge for when software starts doing the work?
That doesn’t mean AI agents won’t be enormously profitable. In fact, the opportunity may be larger than the traditional software market precisely because agents can perform work rather than merely support it. But it does suggest that the next generation of AI winners will need more than impressive models. They’ll need the discipline to allocate intelligence efficiently, and the ability to show that a completed job was worth what it cost to complete.
The smartest agent isn’t necessarily the most valuable one. The most valuable agent is the one that knows how to get the job done and when to stop spending money doing it.
The new AI employees may never ask for a raise. But if we need a dedicated finance department to monitor its expenses, an engineering team to optimize its workload, and a manager to decide when it’s spent enough time on a task, perhaps managing digital employees isn’t so different from managing human ones after all.

articles.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22. In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

articles.title: Could AI Make Fractional CFOs The Future Of Finance?
articles.query: site:forbes.com "artificial intelligence" (trading OR "stock market" OR portfolio OR "hedge fund")
articles.text:
Is finance the next frontier for AI efficiency? Siqi Chen, founder and CEO of CFO.ai—formerly known as Runway—thinks so. The same revolution that AI brought to the coding world, he said, will soon be empowering financial professionals.
Chen said that as fintech works more effectively with AI, more CFOs will be able to take a less traditional path and work fractionally for several companies. And smaller companies will also be able to take advantage of the benefit of working with a trained and competent CFO. Chen tells me more about what he sees as the fractional CFO future later in this newsletter.
This is the published version of Forbes' CFO newsletter, which offers the latest news for chief finance officers and other leaders focused on the budget. Sign up here to get it delivered to your inbox every Tuesday.
Unsurprisingly, inflation remains persistent . October prices increased about 0.4% above those in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics . (There is no baseline year-over-year rate because a government shutdown prevented data from being collected in October 2025.) The largest increases were in fuel oil (up 2% from September), gasoline (up 1%, with a year-over-year increase of 37.4%) and electricity (up 0.9%). All energy costs put together were up 0.7% from September, a slower increase than the 5.2% prices jumped between August and September. According to BLS, most things increased in price last month—used vehicles and communications did not—and even without volatile food and energy costs, prices were up 0.3% in October.
At first glance, October’s job numbers , published Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, look more encouraging. But then a closer look shows that the economy is not in the best place . There were 165,000 positions added in October—well above the 59,000 analysts expected—and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, down a tenth of a percent from September.
But the number of people working part-time, though they want full-time jobs, rose last month by 339,000, and totals 4.8 million . This group of people has either had their hours cut or cannot find full-time work. Forbes’ senior contributor Rachel Wells writes these workers pull the greater economy down. They either are not making the income they need, or are receiving unpredictable income from varying freelance projects or working hours. Regardless, they’re less likely to make big purchases and feel financially stable.
In the midst of all these reports—plus a decisive midterm election that will put control of both houses of Congress into Democratic hands— the stock market has wobbled in the last week . After stocks rose last Wednesday on optimism about the election, they crashed Thursday and Friday as investors feared Democrats would be less open to the expansive—and extremely expensive—AI infrastructure developments. Stocks began to rebound on Monday. (The exception was Nvidia, which fell more than 11% this week following news that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and is being investigated by the company’s board.) But following Tuesday’s inflation report, many stocks dropped, with the Nasdaq losing more than 1% so far.
This time, the polls were right . Americans across the country voted in Democrats in large numbers during last week’s midterm election, flipping the balance of power in both houses of Congress, as well as ensuring a majority of states will have Democratic governors.
Nearly half of all eligible voters cast ballots this year, according to University of Florida political scientist Michael McDonald, making it the best midterm turnout since 1914 . Exit polls showed that voters were motivated by President Donald Trump’s tariffs and immigration policy, writes Forbes senior contributor Stuart Anderson, as well as issues of affordability. And considering how important this is to voters, Forbes contributor Chastity Murphy writes , elected officials can’t afford to fail.
Trump’s unilateral tariff policy has been in congressional crosshairs since the beginning of his second term, since taxation power is supposed to be chiefly wielded by the legislative branch. And while a Democratic Congress is likely to quickly change some of Trump’s policies—like the 50% tariffs on Canada— it’s not clear how much they will be able to accomplish across the board , Forbes’ Alison Durkee writes . Some changes to tariff policy could face opposition from Republicans in the Senate—which will have enough members to filibuster—but it’s worth remembering tariffs might also be supported by Democrats looking to protect jobs in the U.S.
As far as taxation goes, Democrats may look at new taxes on businesses and high earners in order to find money to pay for these projects—and not bog down the people they are trying to help, writes Forbes senior contributor Howard Gleckman. But they are likely to carefully choose their targets. A California ballot initiative to tax billionaires failed last week, with 52.8% of voters supporting it and 47.2% voting against—and that may color how Congress moves forward.
However, Forbes senior contributor Mayra Rodriguez Valladares writes , a Democratic Congress will tighten regulatory control on banks and other financial institutions . And that in turn will bring transparency to a system that has become murky with dealings in private credit, private equity and non-bank financial systems.
There are also big plans to make healthcare more affordable, rolling back cuts to Medicaid and Affordable Care Act subsidies . Forbes senior contributor Joshua Cohen writes these may also face an uphill battle, since Trump would be likely to veto this kind of legislation—though there may be small policy shifts that get through.
AI platform company Anthropic is seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation when it goes public later this month— potentially setting up the largest-ever IPO , according to a new filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company plans to sell 825 million shares at a $70 to $78 price range, and will also be raising funds from executive and founding members’ shares, as well as common stock as part of a private placement deal with large investors including Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Alphabet. Sources told CNBC Anthropic plans to make its market debut next week, on Nov. 19.
If Anthropic lives up to its expected value when it goes public and stokes investor enthusiasm, it could shatter the record set by SpaceX’s $2.1 trillion IPO in June.
In the last year and a half, the use of AI for writing code has exploded , radically changing a software engineer’s productivity and allowing for new programs and applications to be built in a fraction of the time.
Siqi Chen, CEO and founder of cfo.ai, said he sees something similar happening with AI for finance today.
“AI has gotten to a point where it can actually happen,” he said. “...I think that’s going to play out very similar to the way engineering’s played out, where everyone gets to do more exciting things, the team will probably be leaner—but also the people who are ahead of the curve with the most leverage will get paid more and will be in more demand than ever.”
Chen’s company rebranded from Runway to cfo.ai in September, and their main offering is an AI CFO that can work with small companies and fractional CFOs, both performing the necessary calculations, but also explaining what’s happening and alerting important changes. Chen said AI tools like his are expanding the market for fractional CFOs , creating opportunities for qualified financial professionals to more easily and competently balance the work for several smaller companies—as well as get paid more by expanding what they can do. It also opens the door to much smaller companies to bring a CFO aboard, Chen said.
It’s taken some time to create AI-powered fintech applications that do sensible work without burning a ton of tokens . Modern financial work tends to operate in spreadsheets—which can already be automated with formulas and actions to get the correct answers. But spreadsheet automation is strictly deterministic; it will offer one correct answer every time. Generative AI, on the other hand, draws on a host of available sources to generate a contextual answer. And even a basic AI query on your typical corporate financial spreadsheet, Chen said, can translate to a really long and complex query that burns a bunch of tokens for little benefit.
Tools that apply AI in ways it makes sense to finance, however, unlock a new layer of efficiency to the CFO , Chen said. It doesn’t take as long to keep up with the straight financial part of the books, which Chen called low-leverage work. A CFO can instead spend time reviewing the finances, using the human expertise and judgement that AI doesn’t have. And with this depth of assistance from AI, a seasoned CFO can put themselves out as a fractional CFO-for-hire, Chen said, increasing earning potential.
“There’s a real chance that the future of all work is fractional: designers, engineers,” Chen said. “If everyone can just do more, perhaps it makes sense that we get to a point where a lot more people are service providers, and they’re…injecting their unique expertise and judgment across more companies, and everyone gets paid more doing that.”
Fractional and interim executives are in high demand at a variety of companies. According to Heidrick & Struggles , CFO is the most in-demand interim position in leadership , making up more than half of all interim requests covered in a 2026 report. Lightcast found that finance dominates fractional roles, which are mainly at smaller companies.
Chen said AI can keep track of different internal nuances at multiple companies, making it easier for a fractional CFO to operate . And while AI has been known to hallucinate, Chen said that the alternative—a human governing what goes on a spreadsheet—isn’t error-proof either.
“It’s actually already pretty much a lot more accurate than humans in most cases,” he said.
In the AI boom, it seemed that Nvidia could do no wrong—until CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy over the weekend, and investors are mulling the very real possibility that the company’s founder could be ousted by the board. Here’s a look at what investors should watch for —and why it’s important to separate a company’s value from its founder and leader.
At training sessions, new tech tools seem like they can solve many issues that financial employees face. But oftentimes, weeks later many employees have the same problems—and aren’t using the tools to solve them. Here’s how to make these kinds of training sessions actually work and get employees throughout the department to make better use of technology.

articles.title: Deep Learning for Operator Maps in Optimal Liquidation
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: We analyze the solution map of a optimal execution problem in which price dynamics are subject to a general transient impact kernel. Given the structure of the optimal trading strategy derived by Abi Jaber and Neuman in \cite{https://doi.org/10.1111/mafi.12465}, we show that the strategy is locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to the underlying model parameters governing temporary and transient price impact as well as the fundamental price process. Continuity of this map justifies the application of neural-net based approximations which take model parameters as inputs. We propose a method generating samples of the transient price impact kernel for the purposes of creating training data, and a method of projecting the kernel to a finite dimensional representation appropriate for input to a neural net, and a dimensional reduction based on the relationship between inventory and trade signal. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the trained neural net and use it to quantify the potential financial costs associated with misspecifying the transient impact kernel.
