articles.title: ChatGPT Claws Back AI Market Share From Competitors, Study Finds
articles.query: site:forbes.com ("generative AI" OR ChatGPT OR LLM) (finance OR bank OR investment OR insurance OR trading)
articles.text:
Traffic to ChatGPT’s mobile app and website have surged this year after a period of stagnation, and the leading AI chatbot has actually slightly increased its market share over rising competitors like Claude and Gemini, a study by AI growth firm Graphite and market intelligence firm Similarweb published Monday found.
ChatGPT’s mobile app and website notched an all-time high of 61 billion user sessions worldwide in September, Graphite and Similarweb’s study found, a month-over-month increase of 3% and a surge of 24% since September 2025, when the chatbot was in the midst of a traffic slump.
The chatbot also accounts for 81.2% of all AI chatbot sessions worldwide as of September, the study says, a rebound from its all-time low market share of 80.42% in June, whereas none of its competitors have reached 10% of chatbot market share.
Its market share in the United States also ticked up over that same period, rising from a low of 79.64% in June to 80.68% in September.
ChatGPT—which has long been the dominant AI chatbot—lost about one percentage point in worldwide AI market share between January and June of 2026 as competitors like Claude gained ground, but it recovered about 0.27 percentage points from July through September.
OpenAI’s chatbot, though, is still far from the near-total dominance of its early days, which peaked at a 96.11% share of the worldwide AI market in December 2024, according to the study.
ChatGPT appears to be recovering from an apparent period of stagnation—its number of sessions languished from July 2025, where it recorded about 53 billion sessions worldwide, until June 2026, when it also recorded 53 billion sessions before increasing each month after.
Ethan Smith, CEO of Graphite, suggested the chatbot’s traffic increase could be a result of the “cumulative sum of various product improvements and enhancements.” The same month ChatGPT’s traffic began to turn around in June, ChatGPT released its GPT-5.6 models, which was then considered its most advanced and saw a limited rollout at the behest of the U.S. government over concerns about its capabilities. OpenAI then released new GPT-6 models in September. Smith also said ChatGPT users are “returning more” as the technology is “becoming a part of people’s everyday life.” Data from Similarweb, previously reported by Forbes, indicates ChatGPT has much more user loyalty than its competitors. Data shared with Forbes in October showed 64.1% of ChatGPT’s users were exclusive to that chatbot, while just 26.4% of Claude users and 54% of Gemini users exclusively used that chatbot. Gil Luria, managing director and head of technology research at investment firm D. A. Davidson, also previously told Forbes ChatGPT was able to build user loyalty early as the first major AI chatbot to break through to consumers. “That has helped ChatGPT that they were early, got a big install base of consumers that are still happy using ChatGPT, and therefore are habituated to use that,” Luria said.
Even though ChatGPT is increasing its market share over leading competitors Claude and Gemini, the latter two chatbots have surged in use at rates higher than ChatGPT. Worldwide sessions for Claude’s web and mobile platforms surged from 271 million in September 2025 to 5.4 billion in September 2026, a year-over-year increase of over 1,900%. Over the same period, Gemini usage rose from 1.3 billion sessions to 3.7 billion, a 182% year-over-year increase. Claude’s share of the worldwide AI chatbot market jumped from about 0.72% in January to 7.2% in September, the study found, while Gemini’s market share slightly increased—from 4.15% to 4.92%—over the same period. But other chatbots, including Grok, Perplexity and DeepSeek, all lost market share throughout that time.
The United States accounts for just a fraction of worldwide AI chatbot use, the study found. Only about 8.8% of all AI sessions in September 2026 were in the United States, according to the study. But even in the United States, ChatGPT maintains a similar dominance over the market, accounting for about 80% of all AI sessions in the country.
ChatGPT’s traffic has surged in recent months, despite a spate of negative press, including former staffers warning of doomsday scenarios and the attack on AI startup Hugging Face technology by OpenAI agents in July. OpenAI called it an “unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” while CEO Sam Altman said in September it is still the “most severe event we’ve seen,” though reports have since indicated that rogue OpenAI technology meddled with U.S. government websites and Australia’s health care website. A stark claim by Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI and Anthropic staffer, that AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade” also went viral and renewed concerns about the power of AI technology. Voters also rejected AI in Tuesday’s midterm elections, siding against data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives nationwide. Some of the Democratic candidates who won crucial races Tuesday also ran on an anti-data center platform, including Senator-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, who derisively branded her opponent, Sen. Darline Graham, “Data Center Darline.” Luria previously told Forbes consumers are still using ChatGPT despite the security incidents and negative press because OpenAI and its rivals are “thoroughly tarnished.” He said OpenAI and Anthropic have “both been associated with bad outcomes and bad behavior,” but users are “looking past that because the models are so powerful and potent.”

articles.title: China Blocks $5.4 Billion ABB Robotics Deal With Billionaire Masayoshi Son’s SoftBank
articles.query: forbes.com/asia/feed/
articles.text:
China blocked the proposed sale of ABB’s robotics unit to Japanese billionaire Masayoshi Son ’s SoftBank Group, derailing the investment firm’s push into physical AI.
An agency that reviews foreign investments for security in China rejected the $5.4 billion deal, ABB said in a statement , adding that SoftBank has informed the Swiss company of the regulator’s decision. “The Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review in China has prohibited the acquisition of the ABB Robotics business in China,” ABB said. “ABB and SoftBank are in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction.” ABB’s robotics business—employs 7,000 people spread across manufacturing hubs in China, the U.S, and Sweden—booked $313 million in EBITDA on $2.3 billion revenue in 2024, compared with $385 million and $2.5 billion in 2023, according to a statement in October 2025 when the deal with Softbank was announced. Softbank agreed to buy ABB’s robotics unit as part of the Japanese firm’s bid to integrate AI apps with physical AI and boost earnings. The acquisition was expected to be completed by mid to late 2026. Physical AI is “Softbank’s next frontier,” Son, chairman and CEO of Softbank, said in a statement in October 2025. “Together with ABB Robotics, we will unite world-class technology and talent under our shared vision to fuse artificial super intelligence and robotics—driving a groundbreaking evolution that will propel humanity forward.” Son has been expanding rapidly into AI in recent years. He has committed to invest in the $500 billion Stargate AI infrastructure project in the U.S., in partnership with OpenAI, Oracle and MGX. Softbank is also a major investor in OpenAI with $65 billion in cumulative investment as of October.
Prior to the proposed ABB Robotics takeover, SoftBank set up Robo HD, a new holding company that owns its robotics assets comprising over a dozen portfolio companies from Agile Robots SE and Skild AI. In 2024, SoftBank Group announced a joint venture with Riyadh-based investment firm Alat, for manufacturing industrial robots.
Son has net worth of $45.5 billion based on Forbes real-time data, making him Japan’s second-richest tycoon.

articles.title: DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: Existing evaluations of AI models on high-finance work focus on retrieving answers from financial documents and producing numerically correct outputs. Real private equity (PE) and investment banking (IB) work also depends on choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions, and keeping every step auditable. We introduce DeepFinance, an ultra long-horizon benchmark of 21 end-to-end PE and IB tasks that take a human professional an average of 27.1 hours. Each task pairs a request with a data room averaging 19 files and is graded against an average of 84 expert-written rubric criteria covering output, workflow, and judgment. We evaluate 22 model configurations, each in its native agent harness. The best configuration, GPT-6 Astra with max reasoning, satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision-relevant evidence without acting on it.

articles.title: Track or Follow? A Jev-Compatible Multi-Agent Trading System When Web News Lags the Market
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: LLM agents increasingly trade on the Web news they read, yet much Web news about listed firms is published after, and about, the price move it reports, so a reader can agree with the market by following it instead of reading the event. We ask whether LLM judgments of Web news track the market's reaction to the reported event or follow it. To answer, we built a multi-agent trading system whose agents share only point-in-time stores and answer typed questions through the interface of Jev, a hosted typed decision model; code sets every position under a proved bound on how far text can move it. In a hash-committed test of a Jev-compatible reader built from a pinned LLM's option probabilities, item judgments track announcement-window abnormal returns (weekly Spearman 0.119), also after the LLM's release, and event types agree with the issuers' 8-K filings (AUC 0.833); Jev's judgments of news published after its own release track the reaction as well (descriptive). Exploratory analyses show where the association comes from: 72% of earnings news items appear after the issuer's filing, contributor-written items often report the price move, and from the first trade after publication the association falls to 0.023. At a weekly horizon, the confirmatory test detects no rank information over code-only features. Under attack, decision cards traced 88% of successful attacks to the planted item. We propose that market-graded tests of Web-text readers report the criterion from publication, not only from the event.

articles.title: Towards Robust Reinforcement Learning Market Making: Lessons from Loss Function Experimentation
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Market makers play a vital role in ensuring efficient trade within financial markets. Recent literature has delved into training market-making systems using reinforcement learning. This paper delves into the impact of various loss function formulations on risk management behavior within reinforcement-based market making. Through empirical evaluation, we contrast profit-maximizing strategies with risk-averse approaches, finding that penalties for inventory and cash management foster more resilient and adaptable market-making strategies. Our results underscore the significance of striking a balance between profit maximization and risk management in algorithmic trading, providing actionable insights for refining strategies in practical settings.

articles.title: Hard to Fool: A Bounded LLM Research Loop for Quantitative Finance, and What Two Dozen Campaigns Found
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Agentic research loops that let a language model propose a change, run a fixed experiment and keep whatever improves the metric work well in machine learning. In trading research the same loop is a machine for producing false discoveries: a backtest that "improves the metric" is, by default, overfit, look-ahead, a multiple-comparisons artifact, cost-free, or market drift wearing a strategy. We describe Autonomous Quant Researcher, an open-source loop built on the opposite premise: the model proposes, and only trusted code decides. Proposals are strict declarative JSON over a fixed vocabulary, so there is no model-written code to sandbox. Evaluation runs on immutable chronological stores split into discovery, validation and a final holdout that can be opened exactly once, after a durable receipt is written. Acceptance is a conjunction of absolute gates (positive edge and net P&L after costs, a positive weekly-cluster bootstrap lower bound, survival at elevated costs, per-year stability and sample floors), never a single score. Duplicates are refused before they spend a trial, and every formulation, refusal, crash and result is kept in a hash-chained, append-only ledger. We report every campaign run to date, across 0DTE options priced from traded option bars, overnight SPX verticals, daily ETF rules, technical-analysis premises, Kalshi crypto binaries, earnings options, off-exchange volume and a pre-registered alternative-data campaign. Most hypotheses fail, and we report them. Two results survive their pre-registered bars. The clearest example of the loop working is a failure: a language-model survivor that passed discovery and validation with Sharpe ratios near 3 and fell to 0.26 on its single holdout use. The value of such a loop lies less in what it finds than in how hard it is to make it report something that is not there.

articles.title: How To Use AI For Stock Trading Without Following The Crowd
articles.query: site:forbes.com "artificial intelligence" (trading OR "stock market" OR portfolio OR "hedge fund")
articles.text:
When asked to name the best U.S. large-cap growth stocks, AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude may often recommend the same popular companies, such as Nvidia and Microsoft. This reliance on public data creates a crowded trade, where millions of investors receive identical advice and latecomers may face substantial losses. Generative AI excels at organizing known information and screening financial data, but it cannot reliably predict the future or identify unique market advantages. Investors should avoid using chatbots as autonomous advisers to pick individual investments. Instead, artificial intelligence functions best as a research tool to evaluate opportunities, analyze risks and challenge existing investment theses. Ultimately, maintaining independent thinking and valuation discipline remains essential for successful investing.
A few weeks ago, at the peak of New Hampshire’s fall foliage season, a friend asked ChatGPT to recommend the best hike in the state. Its top pick was Artist’s Bluff, near Franconia Notch. When my friend arrived, the trailhead looked like a stadium entrance ten minutes before kickoff. Hikers moved single file, nearly shoulder to shoulder, along a roughly 1.5-mile loop that spends most of its length in the woods and saves its main scenic reward for the summit. Rather than join the line, my friend walked across the street to a ski mountain and discovered a maintenance road that zigzagged up the slope, offering panoramic views the entire way. ChatGPT never mentioned it.
The experience illustrates a growing concern about one of the fastest-growing uses of artificial intelligence in personal finance: asking what stocks to buy. AI can assist with that analysis, but it cannot reliably tell you how an unpredictable future will unfold.
Platforms such as ChatGPT and Claude can evaluate financial statements, summarize earnings calls, compare companies and suggest stocks in seconds. Work that once took hours now takes a single prompt. That is genuine progress. But consider what happens when millions of investors ask these tools essentially the same question: “What are the best stocks to buy right now?”
To test this idea, a colleague and I independently asked ChatGPT and Claude the same straightforward question: “What are the best U.S. large-cap growth stocks to buy now?” My two searches produced identical recommendations. Of my colleague’s two searches, one returned the same five stocks, while the other differed slightly. The recurring names were Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon.
These are exceptional companies, but that is precisely the point. AI identified five of the most widely followed businesses in America. The recommendations may be perfectly reasonable, but where is the investment advantage in receiving substantially the same answers as everyone else? A great company is not necessarily a great investment, particularly when its popularity is already reflected in its valuation.
The models draw on overlapping public data, analyst commentary and prevailing market narratives. Similar questions can produce similar answers, potentially directing investors toward the same securities.
The dynamics of a crowded trade are familiar. Early buyers benefit as later investors push prices higher. Late arrivals pay valuations that already reflect widespread enthusiasm. Eventually returns depend more on finding the next buyer than on improvements in the underlying business. When sentiment reverses, the same crowd heads for the exits at once.
The evidence on concentrated retail attention is sobering. Brad Barber, Xing Huang, Terrance Odean and Christopher Schwarz, writing in the Journal of Finance in 2022 , found that the stocks Robinhood users bought most heavily each day went on to underperform by an average of 4.7% over the following 20 trading days. That study concerned attention-driven trading on a brokerage app, not chatbots. Nevertheless, the underlying risk is similar: when large numbers of investors concentrate their attention on the same securities, those arriving late may face substantial losses.
The risk is not uniform. If a chatbot tells a million people to buy Apple, their orders may barely register against its daily trading volume. The immediate price impact is potentially much greater in smaller companies, thematic names and less-liquid securities, where concentrated retail flows can move prices substantially. Yet even the largest technology companies are not immune to the risks of crowded positioning and excessive valuations.
Generative AI is exceptionally good at organizing what is already known. Markets reward investors who correctly anticipate what is not yet reflected in prices. Identifying what is popular is fundamentally different from identifying what will become valuable before others recognize it.
None of this means investors should avoid AI. Quite the opposite. I believe it is among the most powerful research tools available. Its greatest contribution, however, is probably not picking tomorrow’s winner. It is helping investors evaluate opportunities and risks far more efficiently.
Avoiding losers matters as much as finding winners. AI can screen for slowing revenue growth, deteriorating cash flow, rising leverage, surging capital expenditures and valuations that depend on unusually optimistic assumptions.
Consider a technology company whose spending is growing far faster than its revenue. AI can surface that relationship in seconds and help an investor ask whether expectations have become unrealistic. Ironically, at the time of this writing, Anthropic, OpenAI and even Coreweave have all faced concerns about the sustainability of rising debt levels and future capital spend.
AI can evaluate combinations of profitability, valuation, balance sheet strength and earnings revisions across thousands of securities, surfacing candidates that would otherwise escape attention.
Coreweave, is again, a case in point. Until recently, this high flying stock data center company was a Wall Street darling. Recent attention on its rising debt levels and debt costs with spreads approaching distress levels have brought new focus on this issue that can be applied against thousands of other companies.
AI can review earnings transcripts, regulatory filings and management commentary for shifts in tone or emerging concerns. But sentiment is not value. Some of the best opportunities appear precisely when sentiment is most negative.
Automated systems can monitor predefined conditions, submit orders and enforce risk rules. But speed is not intelligence. A poorly designed strategy executed in milliseconds loses money just as efficiently as it places trades.
These uses improve the investment process without surrendering decision-making authority.
AI’s usefulness depends on the quality and timeliness of the information provided, and the investor’s willingness to challenge its conclusions. Even the most closely followed companies can surprise markets when earnings, spending plans or guidance differ from expectations. An analysis that appeared persuasive yesterday may require substantial revision today. The goal is to build a repeatable research process that incorporates new information while preserving independent judgment.
These four steps can help investors turn AI’s analytical capabilities into a practical workflow while keeping responsibility for investment decisions firmly in their own hands.
AI can examine how companies performed through past rate cycles, recessions, technological transitions and volatile markets. But the future rarely repeats the past. Competitive landscapes change, new technologies disrupt incumbents, policies shift and management teams surprise. Models trained on historical relationships can fail precisely when those relationships break down.
Generative AI also tends to present conclusions with considerable confidence, even when the assumptions are shaky or the information incomplete. That is a dangerous combination: sophisticated explanations that convey more certainty than the evidence justifies. A polished recommendation is not necessarily an accurate one.
Professional investors must distinguish between what is known, what is assumed and what remains genuinely uncertain. That discipline does not come from a prompt.
Chatbots tend to recommend what is already well documented. Investment opportunities that are difficult to identify through conventional research may be less likely to attract widespread attention.
In more than three decades of studying entrepreneurial businesses and managing investments, I have found that some of the most valuable opportunities come from exactly those qualities. In my own work I emphasize what I call the Entrepreneur Factor: the influence of a Founder CEO, entrepreneurial decision making, innovation and a company’s capacity to reinvent itself.
These characteristics rarely show up clearly in historical financial statements or consensus forecasts. An experienced investor may recognize a management team’s ability to create new markets, transform a business model or build advantages that are hard to quantify long before the numbers confirm it.
Successful investing depends not on whether a company is attractive, but on whether its future will exceed what the market already expects. A terrific company can be a terrible investment at an excessive valuation. An unpopular company can be an outstanding investment when its prospects are far better than prevailing expectations. That distinction, between good businesses and good investments, is where experience, independent thinking and valuation discipline remain indispensable.
Use ChatGPT, Claude and similar tools to examine financial statements, challenge assumptions, compare valuations, identify risks and accelerate research. Ask AI why a thesis might be wrong, not merely why a stock might rise. Use it to identify the assumptions embedded in a valuation and the developments that could invalidate them.
But be cautious about letting a chatbot select your investments without substantial independent analysis. The danger is not only that AI might give you a wrong recommendation. It is that it might give the same reasonable-sounding recommendation to millions of other investors.
As AI adoption spreads, I believe independent thinking, professional experience, valuation discipline and judgment will become more valuable, not less. The investors who distinguish themselves will not be those who use AI most often. They will be those who use it intelligently while keeping the independence to challenge conventional wisdom.
The most popular destination is not necessarily the best one. Sometimes the superior opportunity is directly across the street, overlooked by nearly everyone.
Absolutely not. AI models draw on historical data and patterns that may not reliably predict future behavior. Competitive conditions, investor expectations and market relationships can change abruptly, undermining even a persuasive analysis. Investment managers who claim that AI guarantees stock market profits should be viewed skeptically or avoided altogether.
In the U.S., retail investors can legally use AI to research companies, analyze public financial information and inform trading decisions. Many investors already incorporate these tools into their research. The same rules against insider trading, market manipulation and other unlawful conduct apply regardless of the technology used.
Start with curiosity: ask questions, explore the answers and use what you learn to ask better questions. Read expert opinions, then challenge AI to assess their internal consistency, identify critical assumptions and develop opposing arguments. AI can help explain the potential risks and returns of different investment options, but its assessments require verification. Use the process to develop your understanding and judgment before committing capital.
Disclosure: Joel Shulman Ph.D, CFA is the founder and chief investment officer of ERShares, portfolio manager of the XOVR ETF and a professor of entrepreneurship at Babson College. He is also the Founder/CEO of SignalMarkets, a Prediction Market company

articles.title: CosmosAlpha: Multi-Relational Graph Search with Pareto-Guided Exploration for LLM-Driven Alpha Mining
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Discovering predictive alpha factors from noisy financial data is a fundamental yet challenging problem in quantitative finance. LLM-driven formulaic alpha mining offers an attractive paradigm by combining interpretable symbolic expressions with iterative generation and refinement guided by quantitative feedback. However, existing generation-centric and tree-based search strategies primarily organize factors through generation lineage, leaving structural and statistical relationships across search branches underutilized. Consequently, information remains localized along parent--child trajectories, which can confine exploration to redundant regions. Moreover, effective factor discovery must account for multiple distinct objectives that cannot be adequately captured by a single search criterion. We introduce CosmosAlpha, a graph-based LLM factor-mining framework that represents discovered factors as a multi-relational graph encoding generation lineage, expression-structure similarity, and cross-sectional exposure correlation. A Graph Flow mechanism propagates search utilities across the graph, allowing each factor to be assessed using relational evidence from nearby factors rather than in isolation. Pareto-guided selection jointly considers quality, fertility and diversity, explicitly modeling their trade-offs within a multi-objective search framework. Across CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph achieves the best mean rank over seven predictive and portfolio metrics and outperforms its controlled CosmosAlpha-MCTS counterpart on every reported metric, showing a consistent advantage for relational graph search in LLM-driven factor mining. The source code is available at https://github.com/wzhmtldswz/CosmosAlpha

articles.title: Can We Stop the Backtest Yet? Anytime-Valid Promotion Tests for Adaptive Financial Research Agents
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: Financial research agents can generate and monitor trading rules faster than a human can document the resulting selection process. Candidates appear at data-dependent times, weak rules are abandoned, and promising ones are watched until they cross a reporting threshold. We introduce PROMOTE, a protocol that assigns every candidate predictable testing wealth at birth and accumulates a cost-aware e-process only from subsequent returns. If lifetime allocations sum to at most one, a weighted Ville argument bounds the probability of ever promoting a rule whose declared bounded net score has always had nonpositive conditional mean. The result permits dependent candidates, adaptive births, and indefinite monitoring. We audit the implementation in two settings. A retrospective pseudo-out-of-sample replay contains 24 panel--rule hypotheses, 3,000 shared-sign null paths, injected alternatives, and public ETF and industry data. Repeated unadjusted tests produce a family crossing in 94.5% of null paths, versus 0.0% for PROMOTE; at a 15-bp aligned ETF-component perturbation, PROMOTE has 70.1% target power and median crossing session 2,327. A separate exact mean-zero experiment lets an agent select candidate identities and birth times from past scores; the funded gate has 1.77% false-family crossings across 3,000 programs. The market replay produces zero promotions after costs. The certificate controls historical false promotion under the declared null; it is not a certificate that an earlier edge remains profitable at deployment. AI-use disclosure. Generative AI tools, including OpenAI Codex, assisted manuscript preparation. For this preprint version, Codex assisted with LaTeX editing, author and venue metadata, compilation, and layout checks.

articles.title: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection. We propose OLIVIA, a protocol for such tests: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once through a logged lock. We apply it to AI decision models, non-generative language models that return probabilities for typed questions, reading news about S&P 500 stocks: an open-weights model we fine-tuned on 2024-2025 data, three commercial models and standard baselines. The fine-tuned model's signal replicated on two validation quarters (daily information coefficients 0.055 and 0.065) but fell to 0.020 (t = 1.7) on the blinded January-July 2026 test. The commercial models' readings line up with the overnight move to the open (information coefficient 0.074 to 0.077) but not with the move after it, so the news is priced by the time a trader can act on it at the open. No model can tell over- from under-reaction, and no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio. Commercial models identify masked companies in 62% to 74% of cases against a 28% baseline: masking hides names, not companies. The market reads the news first.

articles.title: Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Automated markets increasingly route order flow from learning trading agents through automated market makers (AMMs). We model trader archetypes as AI agents defined by their reward functions and analyze the feedback they create on a constant-product AMM. Herd-dominated and arbitrage-dominated markets of equal size have identical return distributions and turnover, so no rule based on volatility, value-at-risk, stress frequency, or volume can tell them apart; yet their stress episodes differ in length by a factor unbounded in the feedback-to-noise ratio $β/s$. Serial statistics identify the feedback sign from $Θ((s/β)^2\log(1/δ))$ observations, and this rate is tight. When agents trade together, profit-seeking agents ride herds rather than lean against them, leading to all-or-nothing participation. Spread-earning market makers restore stability but make liquidity fragile, with discontinuous collapse and hysteresis; maker--taker pricing, not a uniform fee, is the effective instrument.

articles.title: Beyond Binary Detection: Type-Aware Hallucination Analysis and Hierarchical Detection in Financial Question Answering
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: Large language models are increasingly used to answer questions over financial filings, where an unfaithful answer can mislead investment, compliance, or client decisions. Hallucination detectors are a common safeguard, but they are usually evaluated with a single binary score that reveals neither which kinds of errors analysesed nor why. This paper studies hallucination detection on PHANTOM, a long-context benchmark built from SEC filings, at the level of hallucination type. We first analyze 15,443 paired hallucinated and faithful answers without any detector and find that hallucinated answers are more than twice as long as faithful ones, and that lexical grounding separates the two classes only because faithful answers are bimodal. We then generate hallucinations in nine financially motivated categories, confirm each with a separate verification pass, and diagnose an LLM-based detector on 4,086 usable examples. Generation success varies from 66.3% to 100% across categories. The detector reaches 80.2% binary accuracy but only 44.7% subtype accuracy, never assigns two of the nine categories, and misses between 5.3% and 46.8% of hallucinations depending on category; these misses are unrelated to input length but rise with how far an answer departs from the correct one. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose a two-stage hierarchical detector that first decides whether an answer is hallucinated and then assigns a subtype, raising binary accuracy to 95.6% and subtype accuracy to 56.1%. The results show that type-level evaluation exposes detector weaknesses that aggregate metrics conceal.

articles.title: The Hidden Risk In Automating Financial Models With AI
articles.query: site:forbes.com ("artificial intelligence" OR "machine learning") (compliance OR regulation OR risk) (bank OR financial OR market)
articles.text:
Aritra Pal , CFA, builds machine learning and risk models for regulated banks, with 17+ years in treasury and capital markets tech.
​Every bank I’ve worked at wants to move faster: credit decisions due the same afternoon, forecasts ready before the quarter they cover. I’ve spent more than a decade building machine learning models inside regulated financial institutions, and the failure I’ve come to fear isn’t a wrong number. It’s a model still running smoothly after everyone who understood it has left.
I’ve watched it happen. A model my team built ran in production for months without incident. Then a routine validation review raised a question about a design decision made in the project’s first week, a choice about how certain inputs were structured to work around a gap in the source data. Nobody could fully explain it. The decision made sense at the time, but it was never written down, and the person who made it had since moved to another team. Without that reasoning, we couldn’t satisfy the reviewer, and the model came out of production.
I still think it was a reasonable model. That opinion didn’t count for much. What stayed with me wasn’t really the loss of that one project. It was how little time it took for that knowledge to disappear. According to Gartner , “through 2026, organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects unsupported by AI-ready data.” The reasoning behind a model tends to live in people’s heads rather than in documentation; people move on to other teams, and unless someone deliberately holds onto that reasoning, it leaves with them.
The first question I usually get from leadership on a new AI initiative is which algorithm we’re using. Almost nobody asks where the data comes from, and that’s usually where most of the real work sits. Pulling consistent, reliable data out of six or seven internal systems that were never built to talk to each other takes far more time than most people expect.
One system posts its updates overnight. Another runs a full day behind, and nobody has documented that it does. Every system carries a quirk like that, and someone has to notice it and correct it by hand, usually the same person each time, working from memory rather than a written process.
Automation raises the stakes on all of this. A bad input turns into a bad output faster, with fewer people positioned in the middle to catch it before it reaches a decision. A leader who signs off on an AI initiative without asking pointed questions about the data feeding it is taking on more exposure than the steering committee slide ever shows.
On one project, we tested a heavier, more sophisticated model against a simpler one. The heavier version won, but only by a fraction of a percentage point, and that small edge came at a real cost: It took most of an afternoon every time we had to walk a risk committee through how it actually arrived at a number. We shipped the simpler model instead and kept the more complex one as a challenger to monitor over time.
In a regulated environment, the people accountable for an institution have to be able to sit across from a validator and defend exactly what’s running. A model nobody can fully explain doesn’t clear that bar, no matter how well it scores on a benchmark. I’ve come to treat that as a design constraint that shapes a model’s architecture from the beginning rather than something discovered the hard way during a review.
Most of what changed for me is unglamorous, and the most important piece is just writing decisions down as they’re made, including the ones that feel too small to bother with. Nearly every governance problem I’ve run into traces back to a choice that made complete sense in the moment and none at all once the person who made it had moved on.
That first-week decision about how the inputs were structured was exactly this: a sensible call that lived only in one person’s head, and its absence from any document is the whole reason a working model came out of production. A two-line note at the time would have saved weeks of untangling later.
Explainability belongs in the same place, written into the design document from day one, next to the accuracy targets rather than bolted on before an audit. The test I use is whether a reviewer five years out, someone who never met the team, could follow the model’s reasoning from what’s written down alone. If they couldn’t, the work isn’t done yet.
Monitoring deserves the same forethought. A forecast that looks solid this month can begin drifting the next, and by the time the drift is obvious in the numbers, it has usually been underway for a while. The teams that catch it early are the ones who decided ahead of time what they’d watch and when they’d act.
And then there’s the data work, which needs a real budget and needs it early. It’s the first line finance tries to trim because it doesn’t look like much on a slide, and it’s the thing you’ll miss most when something breaks in a way nobody notices until later.
One last habit is more personal than institutional. Every so often I take one of my own past decisions and try to defend it cold, no warning, the way a validator eventually will. I fail at that more often than I’d like to admit, and I keep doing it anyway.
You can automate a model in a matter of weeks. Keeping it explainable isn’t a phase that ends at launch; it runs for as long as the model itself does, and that work rarely gets a ticket of its own. Someone, eventually, has to stand up and defend what’s running, long after the people who built it have moved on.​

articles.title: The AI Data Center Boom Has A Wall Street Risk Problem
articles.query: site:forbes.com ("artificial intelligence" OR "machine learning") (compliance OR regulation OR risk) (bank OR financial OR market)
articles.text:
A new report by Americans for Financial Reform warns that private equity and private credit are heavily financing the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom, raising concerns if projected revenues fail. Private equity firms already own or finance a significant portion of active U.S. data-center capacity and planned expansions. Traditional banks, insurers, and pension funds are also exposed through direct lending, structured finance, and capital investments. Furthermore, data centers strain local energy grids and water resources while often benefiting from municipal tax abatements. Complex ownership structures can obscure overlapping risks across different assets. Ultimately, analysts question whether financial institutions have accumulated dangerous concentrations in an unproven market.
Private equity and private credit are financing the Artificial Intelligence infrastructure race. If projected returns were to disappoint, however, the consequences could reach banks, insurers, pension funds, and municipal balance sheets.
The artificial intelligence boom is producing one of the largest infrastructure investment cycles in modern history. Yet, behind the construction of massive data centers is a less visible financial story: Wall Street is increasingly financing the land, buildings, power infrastructure, and computing capacity on which the AI economy depends.
A new report by Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, Tracing the Money: Private Equity, Private Credit, and the Data Center Bubble , documents how private equity firms and private credit lenders have become major owners and financiers of America’s data-center industry. Its findings raise an important question: what happens if the revenues expected from AI fail to justify the enormous investments being made today?
The potential consequences extend well beyond technology companies, reaching traditional banks, insurance companies, private credit and equity firms, pension funds, university endowments, utilities, and local governments.
As of December 2025, 78 private equity firms owned or financed an estimated 13 to 17 gigawatts of active U.S. data-center capacity, representing approximately 25% to 30% of the national total. Their portfolios included 670 facilities or campuses. Another 26.8 gigawatts of private-equity-backed capacity was planned, under construction, or in development—more than half of the country’s planned expansion.
The five largest private equity backers identified by the report are Ares Management, Brookfield Asset Management, Blue Owl Capital, DigitalBridge, and Apollo Global Management. Together, they account for approximately 17% of existing capacity and 30% of planned capacity.
The financing requirements are staggering. Morgan Stanley estimates that $2.9 trillion will be spent on new data centers between 2025 and 2028. More than $1.1 trillion is expected to come from private equity, through direct investments, joint ventures, and private credit.
Traditional banks are also involved. The AFR report authors, Iván Cazarin and Dustin Duong, identified JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, PNC, Truist, and Wells Fargo among the notable lenders and financial backers associated with Blackstone’s QTS data-center business.
Approximately one-third of projected data-center investment is expected to be debt-financed. The result is an increasingly leveraged infrastructure buildout involving both regulated banks and less transparent private credit markets.
Major technology companies—including Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle—have increasingly shifted from owning and operating all their data centers to leasing capacity from specialized operators.
This arrangement moves much of the land acquisition, construction, and financing to outside companies, frequently backed by private equity. It can also obscure the full economic commitments associated with the expansion of AI capacity.
The investment thesis assumes sustained growth in AI usage, revenues, and computing demand. Yet the report cites a March 2025 McKinsey study finding that more than 80% of businesses adopting generative AI reported no impact on profitability.
That does not mean AI will fail to generate substantial economic returns. But it highlights the difference between adoption, revenue growth, and actual profitability.
If demand disappoints, data-center utilization, lease economics, and property valuations could weaken. Highly leveraged operators could struggle to service debt or refinancing construction loans. Private credit funds could face defaults and impaired valuations, while equity investors could see expected returns evaporate.
The report identifies more than $200 billion in outstanding loans to AI-related sectors. Two examples show the scale of financing: Blackstone’s private credit arm has provided $12 billion in loans to CoreWeave since 2023; Apollo subsidiary MidCap Financial lent $3.5 billion to Valor Equity Partners in January 2026 to finance its acquisition of infrastructure subsequently leased to xAI.
These transactions illustrate how private credit finances not just technology companies but the infrastructure underlying their operations.
The consequences of a downturn could reach several parts of the financial system:
Banks: Traditional lenders face potential exposure through direct loans, construction and project financing, credit facilities, and relationships with data-center operators. The AFR report identifies major banks among QTS’s financial backers but does not quantify their aggregate AI-related credit exposure. Additional vulnerabilities could arise if banks provide liquidity or financing to funds and companies affected by defaults.
Insurance Companies: Insurers are key drivers in this boom. As I have written previously, they invest in private credit, private equity , infrastructure funds, commercial real estate, and structured credit. They may have direct holdings or indirect exposure through affiliated asset managers, collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), and investment vehicles. A common borrower or sponsor can create concentrations across investments that appear diversified by asset class. The AFR report does not quantify insurer-specific exposure, but its findings make this an important supervisory question.
Pension Funds and Institutional Investors: Public pension funds, university endowments, and other institutional investors supply capital to private equity and private credit managers. Losses could appear as declining fund valuations, impaired distributions, reduced investment returns, and diminished retirement assets. Investors may not know the extent of their exposure to individual data-center borrowers or projects.
Private Credit and Structured Finance: Defaults could affect direct-lending portfolios, infrastructure funds, and CLOs holding loans to exposed borrowers. Fitch recently published a report citing a record-high default rate in private credit. Illiquid assets may also be slow to reflect deteriorating economics, complicating valuations and risk assessments.
Private equity firms frequently own more than data centers. Their portfolios can include natural gas producers, pipelines, power generation, and electricity infrastructure. The same investment managers may therefore benefit from rising data-center electricity demand while financing the facilities consuming that power.
This creates interconnected exposures. If AI demand were to disappoint, data-center operators and energy businesses dependent on their consumption could both suffer.
Physical infrastructure also creates financial risks. Data centers strain electricity grids, require substantial water resources, and can increase local utility costs. The report cites $4.3 billion in residential customer charges for PJM grid connections and attributes $23 billion in customer rate increases to heightened data-center demand.
Water shortages, noise complaints, environmental litigation, permitting restrictions, and community opposition can delay projects or increase operating costs. Approximately 40% of U.S. data-center projects due for completion in 2026 were considered at risk of delay.
Local governments face a different set of risks. Tax abatements can deprive municipalities and states of revenue even as data centers demand expensive infrastructure upgrades. The report estimates that Georgia lost $2.5 billion in tax receipts in one year through data-center tax incentives.
There are also more direct financing concerns. In New Mexico, Doña Ana County issued $4.5 billion in industrial revenue bonds for Stack Infrastructure’s Project Jupiter. The county would own the site and lease it back to the project. This structure raises questions about the allocation of risk among public entities, bondholders, developers, and private investors.
If projects are delayed, abandoned, or underutilized, municipalities could face difficult questions about infrastructure commitments, foregone tax revenue, and the ultimate costs borne by residents.
Perhaps the report’s most important contribution is its examination of private equity’s complex ownership structures. Investment managers can control companies through subsidiaries, joint ventures, partial stakes, and private credit arrangements. These structures make it difficult to identify ultimate ownership, related-party transactions, and overlapping exposures.
A single investment manager could have interests in a data-center operator, its energy supplier, and a financing vehicle lending to the operator. Different investors may believe they are diversified while ultimately depending on the same underlying economic assumptions.
This is why conventional asset-class reporting may underestimate correlated risk.
The question is not simply whether AI is a bubble. It is whether banks, insurers, pension funds, and other investors have accumulated concentrated exposures to an infrastructure boom whose profitability remains uncertain—and whether regulators and investors can see those exposures clearly enough to manage them.
The next financial shock need not resemble 2008 to reveal a similar problem: risk can accumulate in complex financing structures, spread across institutions, and become visible only after underlying asset values begin to fall.

articles.title: Right Numbers, Wrong Questions: Evaluating LLMs on Underspecified Financial Queries
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: Financial assistants answer questions that sound factual but depend on what the user leaves unsaid: what a data figure measures, which product variant is meant, and the investor's situation and the rules that apply. An assistant that ignores these can still answer with a real number from its data, one that answers a different question. We call this frame collapse. We study it in Indian mutual funds, where product variants and tax rules are formally defined, so the correct answer can be computed for every reading. One study tests each challenge. Given an ambiguously labelled figure, models used it, often under the user's label. Given every alternative labelled, they listed them all, but the layout decided which came first. Missing a fact about the investor, weaker agents assumed a default or an outdated tax rule; requiring the fact did not guarantee its use. Because such answers match their data, checks against the data pass them. An AI judge caught mislabelled figures only when told what each field means, and still passed answers that silently chose another reading. We show how these failures arise, not how often, and propose controls for financial assistants.

articles.title: Bank of America kindly asks that you don’t share your banking password with your AI assistant
articles.query: https://techcrunch.com/category/fintech/feed/
articles.text:
Financial giant Bank of America is reminding customers to bank safely by kindly not sharing your banking credentials with your AI agent.
In an email blast to customers titled “Protecting your finances in the Al World,” Bank of America urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, “including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf.”
You can practically sense the frustration in the person sending the email. Still, customers are increasingly handing over their log-ins as personal AI assistants grow more popular . Sharing your banking username and password with an AI assistant runs the risk that it could do something with your finances without your knowledge, or that your bank thinks someone’s raiding your account and locks you out of it. Worse, a security flaw in the AI assistant could result in it leaking your banking credentials elsewhere, giving financially motivated hackers a way into your bank account.
This latest warning comes as banks are still exploring how AI agents fit into the financial world but are reportedly grappling with unauthorized agents accessing their customers’ money . As we discussed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt , banks, payment providers, and processors are still trying to figure out how to allow customers access to their bank accounts using AI tools, such as for agentic payments, which allow people to set agents to autonomously buy things at the best price or the right time.
A spokesperson for Bank of America confirmed the authenticity of the bank’s email that was posted to social media . But heed the bank’s warning, for if things go wrong, it’s on you. Account agreements at most banks hold customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to. “If you do share your credentials,” its email reads, “keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.”

articles.title: A Deep Learning-Driven Operator Splitting Scheme for Free Boundary Problems: An Application to American Option Pricing in Incomplete Markets
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: This paper proposes a deep learning-driven operator splitting scheme for high-dimensional free-boundary problems, with American option pricing as a representative application. In a market with proportional transaction costs, a stochastic liquidity risk with an empirically validated nonlinear drift based on S&P 500 data, and two-factor stochastic volatility, the pricing problem takes the form of a five-dimensional highly nonlinear variational inequality. The proposed scheme decomposes this variational inequality at each time layer into an elliptic continuation equation approximated by a physics-informed neural network and a closed-form projection step enforcing the early-exercise constraint. A conditional $\ell^\infty$ stability bound is derived under stated resolvent and Lipschitz assumptions. The scheme is validated against finite-difference and least-squares Monte Carlo benchmarks, and both the option prices and the learned exercise boundary show close agreement with the reference solutions. Sensitivity analyses with respect to the key model parameters are also reported.
