articles.title: FinLLM-KG: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced LLMs for Financial Sentiment Analysis in Algorithmic Trading
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to predicting the sentiment of each article in isolation and operate as black boxes, which limits contextual understanding and hinders deployment in high-stakes financial decision-making. To this end, we introduce FinLLM-KG, a model-agnostic framework that combines causal LLMs with a financial knowledge graph, in order to inject temporally grounded, company-level knowledge from SEC 10-K filings at inference time, without updating model weights. Within FinLLM-KG, context is supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a small set of relevance-ranked factual triples. This enables sentiment predictions to account for broader firm-level information rather than the article alone, at almost zero computational cost and for any causal LLM. In addition, attributing each article-level sentiment score to individual sentences and to the retrieved knowledge-graph facts makes the evidence behind the prediction inspectable, thereby enhancing explainability and supporting human-in-the-loop review. Simulations demonstrate that FinLLM-KG consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline.

articles.title: AI Debt Risk Is Rising What Retirement Investors Should Know
articles.query: site:forbes.com ("artificial intelligence" OR "machine learning") (compliance OR regulation OR risk) (bank OR financial OR market)
articles.text:
As CoreWeave's bonds fall and its debt reaches $51.6 billion, JPMorgan reports that bank exposure to the AI cloud company is well secured. Roughly $24 billion in bank lending is backed by specific assets like Nvidia chips and data centers, ensuring lenders get paid first. Meanwhile, about $21 billion in parent company debt rests on unsecured promises, trading at 15 percent yields. This unprotected paper is largely held by pension funds, insurance companies, and retirement accounts. A new report notes nearly $4 trillion in AI-linked debt across nine companies, with financial intermediaries shifting risks onto working people.
On Tuesday, with CoreWeave’s bonds in free fall, JPMorgan sent clients a reassuring note. Bank exposure to the AI cloud company, its analysts wrote, is “well managed and very well secured.” Read that sentence carefully. It is not a prediction that CoreWeave will be fine. It is a statement about what happens if CoreWeave is not fine: the banks get paid back first, out of pledged assets, before almost anyone else. Everyone else stands behind them in line. This piece is about who is standing where.
The reassurance was necessary because the numbers are ugly. CoreWeave rents out the computing power behind AI and owed $51.6 billion at the end of June, more than triple its debt a year earlier and now more than the company is worth on the stock market. Its shares have fallen 29 percent this month. Its bonds trade at yields of 15 to 16 percent , the rate lenders charge when they doubt repayment. Insuring $10 million of its debt against default costs more than $1 million a year. Goldman Sachs analysts now call CoreWeave’s bonds the bellwether for the entire AI trade, and the stress is spreading: rivals Nebius and IREN are down 27 and 32 percent this month, and Barclays credit analyst Andrew Keches describes sentiment across tech debt as “decidedly negative.”
Here is what “well secured” means in practice. Roughly $24 billion of bank lending to CoreWeave sits in separate legal vehicles, backed by specific assets: the Nvidia chips, the data centers, the long-term contracts with customers like Meta and OpenAI. The money is released in stages as projects hit milestones. If CoreWeave cannot pay, those lenders do not queue up with everyone else. They take the assets. JPMorgan estimates the largest American banks and Japan’s MUFG hold $1 billion to $3 billion each, mostly in this protected form, and their direct lending to the parent company is limited to a $2.5 billion shared credit line.
Then there is the other pile. About $21 billion of CoreWeave’s debt was issued by the parent company itself, roughly $11 billion of it in convertible notes. No chips or buildings are pledged behind it. It rests on a promise to pay. It is also, in the words of JPMorgan’s own note, the paper “bearing the brunt of the market’s concern.” That is why it trades at 15 percent while the banks sleep fine.
So who holds the unprotected paper? Mostly not banks. Corporate bonds are bought by pension funds, insurance companies, and the bond funds inside retirement accounts. To be exact about it: your 401(k) almost certainly does not own CoreWeave bonds by name. What it owns is the layer CoreWeave’s unsecured bonds sit in, the corporate debt layer that absorbs losses after secured lenders have taken their collateral. And that layer has been absorbing AI paper at a historic pace. Big tech now accounts for about 10 percent of all investment-grade bond issuance worldwide , up from under 1 percent in 2024.
A new report from Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund and the Open Markets Institute , co-authored by Maya Jenkins and Matthew Scherer, counts nearly $4 trillion in debt tied to AI chips and data centers across just nine companies, more than the entire subprime mortgage market at its 2007 peak, with much of it held by pension funds, life insurers, and shadow banks. It is the same conclusion JPMorgan’s note quietly confirms from the other direction: if the losses come, they are not scheduled to land on the institutions that built the structure.
Jenkins, who co-authored the report, does not mince words about who ends up holding that risk:
“Aided by deregulation at the federal level, massive financial intermediaries are shifting the risk from their big AI bets away from wealthy insiders and onto working people,” Jenkins said. “The financial giants anchoring AI infrastructure projects, like Apollo, Blackstone, and BlackRock, are repackaging and selling billions of dollars in AI-linked debt to pension funds, life insurers, and 401(k) providers. Working people’s savings should not be left holding the bag because Silicon Valley can’t pay back their debts. It is time to end the ‘heads they win, tails you lose’ game that Wall Street is playing.”
The IMF mapped the wider loop in its October Global Financial Stability Report : about $950 billion in equity and debt pushed into smaller AI firms, against $1.4 trillion in promised future revenues. I wrote last week about who pays for this boom while it is being built. This is the other question: who pays if the revenues never arrive. Nvidia has even agreed to buy back any of CoreWeave’s unsold computing capacity through 2032, a $6.3 billion backstop that props up the very collateral the secured lenders are counting on. Layer by layer, the structure protects the people who built it.
Max Frumes of the credit research firm 9fin called CoreWeave “absolutely the canary in the coal mine” for AI credit. He is right, but the canary is warning about more than whether something breaks. It is revealing the order in which people get paid when it does.
The honest counterargument: analysts like Talsania argue this is a rates event, not a crack in AI demand. Inflation ran hot, borrowing costs rose everywhere, and leveraged companies always get hit first. Perhaps. But that changes nothing about the line. Calm markets hide who is protected. Stressed markets reveal it. The trigger does not decide who loses. The contracts already did.
About $20.7 billion of CoreWeave’s debt comes due by 2030, and the company will have to borrow again to pay it. That refinancing is the real test. Until then, the most honest sentence of this episode was written by JPMorgan, about its own clients: well managed and very well secured. The banks know exactly where they stand in line. The question is whether the workers and retirees whose money fills the rest of that line know where they stand.

articles.title: The Digital-Energy Recomposition of the Kitchin Cycle: Exploratory Evidence from U.S. IT and Irish Data-Centre Series (1995-2025)
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: Using quarterly FRED and CSO Ireland data over 1995Q1-2025Q4, we examine whether U.S.\ IT investment and Irish data-centre electricity are recomposing the Kitchin cycle around energy- and compute-backed assets. Three findings stand out. First, a Quandt-Andrews sup-Wald test locates a significant break in the U.S.\ IT-GDP correlation at 2014Q3 (sup-W $= 9.69$; $r$ falls from $+0.45$ to $-0.12$); the Fisher $r$-to-$z$ test survives Bonferroni adjustment ($z = +3.11$, $p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.006$), whereas the analogous test on the imposed Cloud-vs-AI boundary does not ($p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.164$), so ``Strategic Decoupling'' pre-dates the AI Era by approximately six years. Second, in Ireland the synchronous AI-Era correlation between metered data-centre electricity and Real GDP is large ($r = +0.41$, $N = 16$) but \emph{collapses to $r \approx 0$ when Real GDP is replaced by Real GNP}, suggesting the headline is largely an artefact of the shared multinational tax-structure footprint between hyperscaler operations and Irish gross output. Third, the Irish cross-correlation profile is asymmetric in the opposite direction to a leading-indicator reading: the largest positive coefficients cluster on the $k < 0$ side (GDP precedes data-centre load), so compute capacity is better read as coincident or moderately lagging. Given the small AI-Era samples and the absence of a quarterly multinational-adjusted aggregate such as GNI*, all coefficients are exploratory; subject to these caveats, the U.S.\ Kitchin cycle is best dated to 2014Q3, and the Irish Energy-Data Nexus is dominated by multinational firm activity.

articles.title: Financial Context-Rich Strategy for Actor-Critic based Agents: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Stock Trading
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: In modern financial markets, more than 3/4th of the large volume trade is executed by algorithmic trading based on advanced trading strategies to attain higher precision and speed than traditional human traders. The conventional strategies focused on price-based indicators are inadequate in capturing the market dynamism arising from real-world events such as social sentiments, political instability, or sudden economic shifts. With the rise of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and data availability, there is a requirement for more efficient algorithms that can incorporate these external factors in trading strategies. DRL has shown potential in simulating real-world scenarios and in simplifying complex decision-making since DRL agents can automate the trading process i.e. executing trades in a manner comparable to human traders. They have shown reliable performance since they can update their policies based on risk and quantitative factors. In this paper, we propose a DRL approach based on partial and deep-infusion of sentimental analysis. It features distinct policy designs of actor-critic-based agents: only policy optimization (A2C & PPO) and policy optimization along with Q-learning principles (DDPG, TD3 & SAC). Our findings reveal, that the agents based on policy optimization combined with Q-learning, significantly and consistently demonstrate improved performance upon sentiment deep-infusion in profit maximization as well as risk-averse trading.

articles.title: When News Gets Old: Portfolio Allocation with Reinforcement Learning and Large Language Models
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Financial news can influence investment decisions long after publication. Timely news may reach an investor before prices fully adjust, whereas older news may already be reflected in prices. We examine two ways to handle aging signals: retain them and give a portfolio policy timing information, or filter them out before portfolio selection. A fixed large language model (LLM) extracts signals from public SEC disclosures. We compare these treatments in reinforcement learning (RL) policies and LLMs that choose portfolios directly. We evaluate returns after trading costs in historical tests over 2023-2025. RL choices respond to timing information in a controlled test, but historical returns show no consistent benefit from adding it. For the LLM, filtering old news produced the highest average net return, reaching 18.43% per year when news delivery was delayed by four weeks. This exceeded the returns of all RL strategies that used news.

articles.title: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine role-specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds, SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven-layer shared memory, assembled by code from the system's own record, gives each decision its position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent's past decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All three operate around an invariant core of order arithmetic, risk rules and discipline-agent prompts that no self-edit can reach. In a five-month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more and lost 1.35 points against the market over five days where the joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was followed; and a 2015-2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control evening. Code: https://github.com/yebof/quant-agent

articles.title: What Prediction-Market Contracts Reveal at Launch: Trading Volume and Dispute Risk
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Using a near-census of 802,863 resolved markets listed on Polymarket between January 2023 and May 2026, and only information available at listing (the market's title and description, named resolution source, and contract metadata), we predict lifetime trading volume and whether settlement is later disputed. Contract information predicts trading volume well (out-of-sample $R^2 = 0.747$ for log volume), and most of the signal is interpretable: market topic provides the largest gain ($+0.289$ $R^2$ over a $0.220$ contract-feature baseline), wording and resolution-rule design add smaller but measurable improvements ($+0.027$ combined), and neural text models add little beyond the interpretable features. This performance does not survive a period of platform change coinciding with a shift in listing formats: accuracy in predicting whether a market reaches \$1,000 falls from AUC $0.940$ under same-period evaluation to $0.577$ when training on past quarters and testing on later ones. The loss concentrates in markets whose question forms were absent from training (76.9% of test markets; on familiar forms the model still reaches $0.778$), and a decomposition attributes more of it to a changed relationship between contract characteristics and demand than to an outdated mapping from text to features. Dispute predictors are more stable but less precise: launch-time features rank dispute risk far better than chance (AUC $0.78$), yet at a 0.31% base rate precision is too low for case-by-case prediction (average precision $0.012$), so the scores suit ranking groups of markets rather than forecasting individual disputes.

articles.title: Lineage-Aware Search Control for LLM-Based Evolutionary Factor Mining
articles.query: arxiv:all:"artificial intelligence" AND (all:finance OR all:banking OR all:portfolio)
articles.text: Formulaic alpha factor mining searches for symbolic expressions that transform market data into predictive signals. Recent LLM-based evolutionary factor mining methods use large language models as semantic variation operators. Under the conventional LLM-EA paradigm, stochastic variation and fitness-based selection can leave the search weakly directed and concentrated around a narrow set of structurally similar factors. We argue that these limitations arise because current methods mainly organize search at the individual and population levels, leaving lineage-level control underused. A lineage connects successive factor variants through evolutionary descent. We propose LineageEvo, which uses lineage in two coupled forms of search control: (1) lineage-conditioned LLM variation, which distills Lineage-Scoped Search Experience into operator-specific priors and fuses them with global operator priors, providing persistent, lineage-relevant guidance for LLM generation; and (2) lineage-stratified search allocation, which balances factor quality against lineage concentration by distributing the search budget across lineages during evolutionary search. Together, these mechanisms make semantic variation more direction aware and prevent branches from dominating the evolution, thereby promoting the discovery of predictive and diverse factors. We evaluate LineageEvo on CSI 500 and S&P 500 in terms of factor predictiveness, portfolio performance, search efficiency, and lineage- and expression-level diversity. LineageEvo achieves the strongest predictive performance on both markets, while LSPS produces a more balanced lineage distribution and a structurally broader factor pool. The results support lineage as a useful intermediate unit for controlling LLM-based evolutionary factor search.

articles.title: LOB-Impact Benchmark: Emergent Market Impact in Generative Limit Order Book Models
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Realistic market impact is essential for generative limit order book (LOB) models to serve as world models for trading agents. If a simulator misprices this mechanism, agents learn policies that are optimal in the simulator but wrong in the real market. Existing metrics assess generated streams purely through distributional comparison with historical data, leaving counterfactual response to an agent's own orders largely unexplored. Here, we show that market impact emerges naturally in neural LOB generators trained solely for next-token prediction. We inject execution-style metaorders into the generated message flow of five autoregressive models across five NASDAQ stocks and measure the response using estimators from the empirical impact literature, validated on baselines whose physics is known in advance. Our benchmark evaluates any message-level generator in three phases: free generation (reading order-flow persistence against price diffusivity); metaorder injection (yielding the impact law's exponent and amplitude); and a post-execution window (measuring relaxation). In addition, comparing each visible injection to a blind, simulator-only control isolates the model's learned response from standard book mechanics. For every model on every stock, we measure how the impact responds as a function of cumulative metaorder participation. Interestingly, we observe emergent impact in generative models of market data, with exponents in the range of 0.63 to 1.21, slightly above the traditional 0.5 of the square-root law of impact. In the family of models tested, we are so far unable to observe impact decay during relaxation. We tentatively attribute this to the still-short context windows of the models. We release the benchmark as open source to validate future generative models for market data.

articles.title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions
articles.query: arxiv:all:"machine learning" AND all:trading AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Trading discipline often fails people. Our study tested whether four AI trading agents followed their strategies and risk rules. Offering traders the evidence and an agent evaluation toolkit to separate luck from following the rules, before giving agents meaningful autonomy or capital. Our study analysed 2,627 closed positions from 12 February to 27 August 2026 across the same asset universe and execution conditions. Most positions were simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee; 18% involved real Hyperliquid orders. Each position declared a strategy, stop and target, with a limit of five open positions per agent. The fleet finished net positive after fees. Rule adherence was high across all four agents, including the unprofitable one. Profitability tracked how often agents won relative to their break-even win rates. Institutional-style controls ran by default and contained losses through a 29% market drawdown and recovery, with documented exceptions. The discipline held for all four agents. Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, and typical losses closed at declared levels. Declared risk remained stable after losses and broadly stable across calm and volatile months. Twenty-three of 24 runs respected the position limit; logs identify the exception's size and duration. The same live data produced different results across assigned strategies. The trade-log tests can be rerun from the published trade snapshot; regime tests also require the published Bitcoin prices and regime labels. Section 3.5 specifies the stop-breach tolerance. These trade-level results are not account-level returns or proof of a lasting edge. Our study provides an evaluation toolkit to help traders distinguish rule-following from luck before committing capital. For anyone considering allocating capital to agents to trade, discipline should be the entry test, not the only test.

articles.title: Trust, But Verify: How Regulators Want Banks To Use AI
articles.query: site:forbes.com ("artificial intelligence" OR "machine learning") (compliance OR regulation OR risk) (bank OR financial OR market)
articles.text:
On October 15, 2026, the Financial Stability Board published a final report outlining 12 sound practices for responsible artificial intelligence adoption in financial institutions. The non-binding toolkit addresses growing risks like complex explainability, autonomous agentic actions, cyber threats, and shadow AI. While case studies show significant gains in areas like fraud reduction and loan default prediction, the report emphasizes that governance must keep pace. Institutions are encouraged to apply these practices proportionately and integrate them into existing enterprise risk frameworks. The guidelines cover organization-wide governance, such as strategic direction and accountability, alongside lifecycle practices ranging from data governance to human oversight.
The Financial Stability Board’s final report sets out 12 sound practices for responsible AI adoption. It is a toolkit, not a rulebook, but boards should read it closely.
Financial institutions have used artificial intelligence for years, yet generative and agentic AI have changed the stakes. On 15 October 2026, the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the body that coordinates financial regulation across major economies, published its final report on responsible AI adoption. It sets out 12 “sound practices” for banks, insurers, asset managers and others.
The report is not a binding international standard, and it does not tell firms whether to adopt AI. It is a practical toolkit that institutions can tailor to their own context and risk profile. Its message to boards is that AI offers real gains, but those gains depend on governance that keeps pace with the technology.
The FSB’s case studies show why firms are moving quickly. One bank’s machine-learning models identified over 95% of non-performing SME loans at least three months before borrowers missed repayments, and more than 80% of the flagged borrowers avoided default. A regional bank cut preliminary credit proposals from more than a day to 15 minutes. A large bank’s agentic fraud system helped reduce card fraud losses by over 20% in the first half of its 2026 financial year.
The report also warns that standing still carries risk. Institutions that avoid AI may lose competitiveness and weaken their ability to detect cyber threats and fraud.
The same technology can amplify existing risks and create new ones. The FSB highlights several concerns:
Two principles run through the report. First, the practices should be applied proportionately. A large, interconnected bank using AI in critical functions should adopt more robust controls than a small firm running a low-risk chatbot. Smaller institutions, and lower-risk use cases, may apply only the relevant practices or adapt them.
Second, firms need not start from scratch. The report encourages integration into existing enterprise risk, operational resilience, cyber, third-party and model risk frameworks. One global systemically important bank profiled in the report chose this route. It embedded AI governance in its established risk structures and added a senior-chaired AI committee for oversight, rather than building a parallel bureaucracy.
Strategic direction. The board and senior management should align AI adoption with the firm’s business model, risk appetite and strategy. That can include drawing hard lines, such as prohibiting fully automated decisions in critical areas where risks exceed tolerance. Boards are also expected to ensure that they and their staff have the skills to provide real oversight.
Governance and accountability. Roles must be clear. Under the familiar “three lines of defence” model, business units own outcomes, risk functions provide independent challenge, and audit delivers assurance. Where one AI monitors another, the monitor must be independent of the system it reviews.
Risk management and documentation. AI risks belong in existing frameworks, with controls scaled to materiality. Firms should keep inventories and lifecycle records. For agentic AI, each agent should have a unique identifier so its actions can be traced.
Organizational adaptability. Governance must keep learning, through staff training, external monitoring and post-incident reviews. The report also warns of workforce deskilling, since over-reliance on AI can erode the judgement needed to oversee it.
The remaining eight cover the life of an AI system, from inception to retirement.
Materiality and risk assessment. Firms should assess each use case at the outset and revisit the assessment as it scales. The report makes a subtle point: a highly autonomous agent performing a low-materiality task can still cause serious harm. For agents, risks from expanded permissions may compound rather than simply add up.
Selection. Firms should weigh business objectives, cost and risk when choosing models. The most complex model is not always the best, and a simpler, cheaper, more explainable system may be enough.
Data governance. Data must be accurate, complete, secure and traceable, with attention to lineage and bias. Agents add a particular risk, because they ingest and reuse data in ways that are hard to detect.
Explainability and transparency. Where possible, firms should favour more explainable approaches. Otherwise they should apply compensating controls and give each audience, from customers to supervisors, appropriate transparency.
Performance management. Continuous validation, monitoring and testing should catch problems such as model drift and hallucination.
Human oversight. Mandatory review and override points should scale with a system’s autonomy and the materiality of its decisions. The report warns that automation bias, meaning excessive trust in machine output, can quietly undermine oversight.
Cyber and ICT risk. AI should be built into security and resilience testing. Threats include prompt injection, data poisoning and deepfakes.
Third-party risk. Oversight must extend to vendor due diligence, concentration, supply-chain dependencies, contractual protections and exit planning. The report notes that firms remain accountable for AI outcomes even when the technology comes from a supplier, and that third-party tools may contain AI the firm doesn’t know about.
The FSB’s stated aim is to help institutions adopt technologies such as generative AI and advanced machine learning while protecting operational resilience, preventing systemic vulnerabilities and preserving financial stability. The report acknowledges that guidance on agentic and multi-agent systems is still immature and will need to evolve.
For executives, the report does not oblige them to do anything. Its value is as a benchmark that supervisors and peers are likely to reference. Institutions that already know where AI is used, who is accountable, how much human oversight each use case needs and what happens if a key vendor fails will be better placed to scale AI safely. Those that cannot answer these questions have a place to start.

articles.title: AFNO: Universal Certifiably-Arbitrage-Free Operator Learning Framework for European Call-Price Surfaces
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Neural operators (NOs) have been introduced as deep learning-powered solutions to the computational bottleneck of solving families of problems. Once trained, an NO can rapidly output approximate solutions, avoiding the need to rerun classical solvers. However, standard NO architectures cannot guarantee static no-arbitrage when predicting European call-price surfaces from market or model features and, as we verify experimentally, can yield negative PnL in downstream trading tasks. We introduce a certifiably arbitrage-free (AF) and universal encoder-decoder NO framework, continuously mapping inputs from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) $\mathcal{H}$ over any fixed subset of $[0,\infty)^2$ to a convex combination of arbitrage-free European call-price surfaces by continuously solving an approximate nearest-neighbour problem. We show that a nearest arbitrage-free correction of an unconstrained predicted surface need not exist, implying that no-arbitrage cannot, in general, be restored through post-processing. Further, we show that standard NOs, such as the FNO and certain encoder-decoder NOs, admit parameter configurations whose outputs violate static no-arbitrage. Thus, out-of-the-box NOs generally cannot be certifiably restricted to arbitrage-free configurations, but may only be guided towards them through PINN-type regularization during training.

articles.title: Why The AI Stock Market May Not Be A Bubble
articles.query: site:forbes.com "artificial intelligence" (trading OR "stock market" OR portfolio OR "hedge fund")
articles.text:
With large-cap stocks surging significantly since late 2022, investors question if an artificial intelligence bubble has formed. A bubble involves implausible valuations likely to implode, yet current price-to-earnings ratios sit near 10-year averages. Although the Shiller CAPE ratio signals an overvalued market, a 2026 paper shows post-1995 accounting changes distort historical comparability. Specifically, immediate R&D expensing and impairment accounting shift the CAPE level upward. Furthermore, robust corporate earnings growth and rising return on equity support current valuations.
Bubbles always implode. - Charles P. Kindleberger , Manias, Panics, and Crashes: A History of Financial Crises
With US large-cap stocks up almost 114% since the end of 2022, equivalent to over 22% annualized and well above the long-term historical return of 10%, investors may ask whether this is an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven stock market bubble. The case gets even more interesting when you look at the technology sector’s nearly 250% total return over the same period, which equates to a whopping 39% annualized return. This article will explore whether investors should fear that markets have entered an unsustainable bubble.
High returns and expensive valuations are necessary but not sufficient conditions to call something a bubble. A bubble is defined as valuations that, after accounting for cash flow, growth, and competitive assumptions, are sufficiently implausible. This implausibility makes a sizable price decline likely, or, in Kindleberger’s words, “Bubbles always implode.” Let’s look at the evidence.
While the S&P 500 has returned almost 20% year-to-date, the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, the cost per dollar of earnings, based on expected 2026 corporate earnings, has fallen. How is that possible? The answer is that S&P 500 earnings are expected to grow 32.4% in 2026, according to FactSet consensus estimates.
When looking at the long-term history of P/E ratios, the current 22.2 times is not cheap, but it is essentially back at its 10-year average. It pays to remember that there are two ways a seemingly expensive asset can get cheaper: 1) the price of the asset can fall or 2) the earnings or cash flow produced from the asset can grow quickly enough to shrink the valuation.
We favor the figures of average earnings covering between five and ten years. – Benjamin Graham and David L. Dodd, Security Analysis , 2nd edition, 1940
While it has long been a common idea among professional security analysts to average several years of earnings to estimate a company’s normalized earnings power through an economic cycle, a paper in 1998 by John Campbell and Robert Shiller popularized the CAPE ratio for investors to judge the outlook for future stock returns based on this valuation. In theory, CAPE uses a rolling 10-year average of inflation-adjusted earnings to reduce cyclical noise and produces a more stable estimate of underlying corporate profitability.
Fed Chair Alan Greenspan did not explicitly cite the CAPE ratio in his 1996 ‘irrational exuberance’ speech. Still, the speech occurred as Robert Shiller’s research on valuation ratios was becoming increasingly influential. The association grew after Shiller’s book Irrational Exuberance used CAPE to argue that equity valuations had reached historically extreme levels.
Shiller published Irrational Exuberance on March 15, 2000, almost exactly at the peak of the dot-com bubble. The S&P 500 peaked on March 24, 2000, then fell 49.2% before bottoming on October 9, 2002. The dot-com-heavy NASDAQ index faced a far worse fate, declining 77.6% from its March 10, 2000 high to its October 9, 2002 low.
The CAPE ratio today suggests a significantly overvalued stock market, and perhaps an AI stock market bubble. Still, it has produced almost constant false alarms since we passed the Global Financial Crisis. A 2026 paper by Dino Palazzo examined why the CAPE ratio, despite its continued popularity, has failed as an indicator.
Palazzo found that post-1995 reported earnings are less comparable to historical earnings. Palazzo traces the structural break, a higher CAPE ratio starting in 1995, to two accounting changes that affected earnings.
FASB Statement No. 2 required companies to expense internally generated R&D immediately. Economically, much of R&D is an investment intended to produce benefits over multiple years. As R&D intensity rises, current GAAP earnings absorb the full expenditure, while historical tangible-capital businesses capitalized substantial investment and recognized it gradually through depreciation. Palazzo finds this is the dominant source of earnings mismatch and CAPE level shift .
SFAS 121 and related changes encouraged faster and more frequent recognition of impairments and restructuring losses. Accounting is asymmetric: impaired assets are written down, but internally regenerated value is generally not written back up. Special items are heavily concentrated in downturns. A single recession-era charge remains in CAPE’s denominator for ten years, so averaging does not remove the distortion. Palazzo finds special items had a smaller impact but added substantial cyclical volatility .
Palazzo’s adjusted CAPE suggests valuations remain elevated but resemble prior long technology and productivity cycles rather than a wholly unprecedented regime. While the paper doesn’t state this directly, it’s fair to interpret his adjustments as suggesting AI hasn’t caused a stock bubble.
With the market so concentrated, over 40% of the S&P 500’s market capitalization weight sits in the top 10 largest companies, it is notable that the 12-month forward estimated price-to-earnings ratio is well below the 2000 tech bubble level. While this does not prove the absence of a bubble, it is strong evidence to the contrary. Further, 29 times earnings is not inexpensive.
Over the long term, it’s hard for a stock to earn a much better return than the business which underlies it earns. – Charlie Munger, Poor Charlie’s Almanack
As noted previously, one way a seemingly expensive asset can earn its valuation is by growing earnings faster. The current AI-driven earnings boom, also evident in the communication services sector via Meta Platforms (META) and Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), is still expected to drive above-average S&P 500 earnings growth through 2027.
If these attractive earnings growth rates materialize, the S&P 500’s valuation becomes much more attractive. Further, the S&P 500’s return on capital, as measured by return on equity (ROE), has been rising and is expected to continue improving. All else equal, investors should be willing to pay a higher multiple for a stock market that delivers higher returns on capital for shareholders.
As with the higher S&P 500 earnings growth rate, all roads lead back to technology. Technology companies’ profitability has been improving and has been a primary driver of the S&P 500’s overall profitability improvement.
Historical earnings growth rates also support the view that this is not an AI-driven stock market bubble.
There remains a legitimate concern about some companies’ earnings running well above their normalized levels, or, in short, overearning. Goldman Sachs expects US AI hyperscalers to spend $800 billion in 2026 and $1.1 trillion in 2027 on capital expenditures to build out AI capacity. For example, this unrelenting AI demand has almost certainly driven earnings for some semiconductor and memory chip producers well above normalized levels. The harder part is knowing when the shortages causing the excess earnings will end. So far, demand growth and AI utilization growth remain intact.
While stocks are clearly not cheap on the surface, their robust fundamentals are not consistent with a stock market bubble. Unlike the 2000s dot-com bubble, current valuations are plausible if the better-than-normal corporate profitability continues. This is a rare instance where the present differs from the past. The dominance of some technology leaders, often across their respective ecosystems at massive scale, keeps earnings power elevated above historical norms. This presupposes that this dominance can last, but right now that looks like the base case.
Stocks are pricing in a pretty rosy outlook, with ROE expected to remain above pre-2021, pre-AI technology-boom norms. Even without a stock bubble, disappointment would likely still lead to stock market declines. Investors should continue to monitor AI-related demand growth and pay particular attention to companies currently overearning, as watching for the turning point is more crucial for this group.
Disclosure: Glenview Trust may own the stocks mentioned within its recommended investment strategies.

articles.title: Fitch's AI Stress Test Flags Sectors Facing The Most Credit Risk
articles.query: site:forbes.com ("artificial intelligence" OR "machine learning") (compliance OR regulation OR risk) (bank OR financial OR market)
articles.text:
Fitch Ratings has published an Artificial Intelligence Stress Test evaluating how adverse AI developments might impact credit profiles over five years. The report concludes that AI does not pose a broad threat to credit quality, as sectors representing most rated debt remain resilient. However, the test identifies sharp pockets of risk in business process outsourcing, media production, software, AI infrastructure, and the private credit vehicles lending to them. Retail banks and business development companies both score 40, though their risks differ. For banks, the threat is a slow shift in business models, while business development companies face potential loan losses, particularly on software borrowers. Fitch reports no AI-driven rating actions to date across these sectors and plans to apply the test to individual issuers later this year.
Fitch Ratings finds that AI is not a broad threat to credit quality. Yet, it flags sharp pockets of risk in outsourced services, media production, software and AI infrastructure, and in the private credit vehicles that lend to them.
Fitch Ratings recently published its Artificial Intelligence Stress Test , assessing how adverse AI developments could affect credit profiles over five years. The headline is reassuring: sectors representing the vast majority of rated debt show resilience. However, the detail is less comfortable. A handful of corporate sectors score between 60 and 80, and the financial institutions that lend to or invest in them carry that risk.
This first phase scores a representative issuer in each of 107 granular sub-sectors across Corporates, Infrastructure, Financial Institutions and Structured Finance. Public Finance and Sovereigns are excluded. Fitch tests three adverse scenarios, each calibrated to roughly a 10% to 20% likelihood over five years. They are not mutually exclusive:
Each sector gets a score from 0 to 100. Fitch stresses that the rating impacts are illustrative and that a score of 40 or more signals the potential for negative rating action for a typical issuer.
The highest scores sit in labor-intensive services, media and software, plus the infrastructure built for AI.
A high score is not a forecast of imminent downgrades. In BPO, rating actions have been muted relative to the score of 80, because many incumbents benefit from high switching costs and deliver services through AI themselves. Issuers with hard-to-replicate services can score below the sector.
The split between the two data center categories shows how Fitch analysts think about over-investment. Cloud data centers in strong markets have a use case beyond AI and typically carry fully contracted leases of 7 to 15 years with highly rated hyperscalers. AI training facilities tend to be remote and used mainly for AI, and Fitch does not rate speculative-build AI data centers. The more exposed group is corporate-rated “neoclouds” that own the chips and sell compute directly. For them, stress would arrive through lower utilization, weaker pricing and customer concentration.
Retail banks, private banks, BDCs, fund finance and investment management organizations all score 40. The difference lies in how stress reaches each one.
Fitch expects direct consequences for banks to be neither widespread nor severe enough to drive sector-wide rating actions over five years. The pressure points are competitive: fee and margin compression in standardized products, and smaller banks that cannot match larger rivals’ AI spending. Corporate and investment banks score only 20 because their franchises rest on client relationships and regulatory barriers. Their main exposure is indirect, through private credit and collateral-dependent financing businesses.
Fitch’s BDC score reflects asset risk. Software is a top industry exposure in many BDC portfolios, and Fitch estimates it at about 20% of portfolios at fair value, with some reported figures understated. Software valuations have already fallen and pressured net asset values. The adverse scenario assumes meaningful software write-offs.
The cushion looks adequate for now. Fitch expects most rated BDCs to keep meeting asset-coverage requirements even if every software investment were written down by 50%. Software loan maturities pick up meaningfully from 2028, and the downside outliers are BDCs with outsized software exposure or elevated starting leverage.
In fund finance, subscription lines are well insulated because repayment rests on uncalled commitments from institutional investors. The vulnerable products are NAV facilities, private equity CFOs and rated note feeders, where fund valuations are the source of repayment. Fitch expects rating pressure to be limited to NAV facilities with tight headroom and to mezzanine or subordinated tranches with concentrated exposure to outsourcing, software, traditional media or legacy financial services.
For asset managers, Fitch does not expect AI to displace investment management. It expects dispersion. Firms that use AI well in research, portfolio construction and risk management could gain ground, while laggards risk client attrition. Fitch scores Investment Management Organizations at 40 but traditional and alternative Investment Managers at 20, reflecting limited asset-quality and business-model risk.
GPU/AI compute ABS has the highest structured finance score at 50. Rapid chip turnover shortens the economic life of collateral, and repayment depends on the lessee. Deals backed by hyperscaler lease payments rest on committed cash flow from an investment-grade counterparty, while monoline compute providers are more vulnerable. Its rated GPU exposures carry no residual value exposure because the notes amortize within the contracted lease term. Elsewhere, overcollateralization, amortization and diversification can absorb a good deal of stress before ratings move. Fitch also flags that broad job displacement could raise delinquencies in consumer lending, credit card and student loan pools.
AI is not a uniform tide for credit, and it is not a threat to regulated banking as a whole. It widens the gap between resilient sectors and exposed business models. For investors and risk managers, the most important question is not whether AI will hurt credit, but who is lending to the sectors it hurts most and how much cushion will lenders hold. Phase 2 should start to answer that.

articles.title: Deep Learning vs. Statistical Models for Multi-Horizon Price Forecasting of Second-Hand Electronics: A Systematic Benchmark
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Forecasting resale prices of used electronics is critical for subscription-based platforms where pricing errors translate directly into risk. Unlike structured financial markets, second-hand electronics exhibit high volatility, sparse listing histories, and non-normal price dynamics - yet no systematic time-series benchmark exists for this domain. This paper presents the first multi-horizon benchmark of statistical and deep learning forecasting models for used electronics price prediction. We use a large-scale dataset of daily price listings from Polish online marketplaces (January 2022 to March 2025, 100+ smartphone and laptop models) and evaluate eleven models across six horizons from 1 to 365 days, covering classical methods (ARIMA, ETS, Theta), recurrent and convolutional networks (LSTM, TCN), and modern deep architectures (N-BEATS, N-HiTS, TFT, PatchTST, Informer). Three complementary evaluation protocols assess trajectory fitness, one-shot endpoint accuracy, and cross-horizon transfer. N-BEATS achieves the lowest MAPE beyond 30 days, reaching 8.51% at 365 days versus 14.94% for the best statistical baseline - a 43% reduction. At short horizons (1-7 days), all models converge near 0.72% MAPE and the naive baseline remains competitive. A single N-BEATS model trained at 365 days generalizes to all shorter horizons, eliminating the need for horizon-specific models. N-BEATS and N-HiTS also demonstrate superior hyperparameter stability.

articles.title: Deep kernel hedging
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: We introduce a deep kernel hedging framework that combines the flexibility of deep learning with the structural inductive bias of kernel methods. The hedging functional is restricted to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space whose kernel is parameterized through a neural network embedding of the input features. The framework minimizes a regularized empirical risk under convex loss functions and can accommodate path-dependent information through truncated time-augmented signature features. We derive a generalized representer theorem for the joint hedging problem, reducing the empirical optimization to a finite-dimensional problem. To further reduce the computational cost associated with large kernel matrices, we develop a scalable random Fourier feature approximation and establish convergence guarantees. The random Fourier parameters are sampled once and remain fixed throughout training, while the deep kernel adapts to market data through the learned neural representation. We evaluate the performance of the proposed deep kernel approach on both synthetic and real data and compare it with standard kernel methods and classical deep hedging architectures. Numerical results indicate competitive and robust hedging performance, particularly in low-data regimes, which highlights the benefits of combining expressive neural representations with the inductive bias of kernel methods.

articles.title: Taming the Greeks: Option Portfolios with Inductive Biases
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: We present an end-to-end deep learning framework for systematic options trading that directly embeds hedging behavior through explicit control of portfolio-level risk exposures. While neural networks trained to optimize risk-adjusted performance have been shown to outperform traditional rules-based strategies, such approaches remain agnostic to the sensitivities of the resulting portfolios with respect to specific underlying risk factors. We propose a general training objective that combines a performance-driven loss with a differentiable risk-sensitivity penalty, enforcing neutrality to selected risk dimensions. Unlike reinforcement learning methods that approximate optimal hedging policies via simulated market dynamics, our framework operates entirely on historical data and jointly optimizes risk-adjusted returns and targeted risk constraints in a single learning problem. We instantiate the framework on static delta-neutral straddle portfolios with the penalty directed at first-order directional exposure, and evaluate two penalty variants -- an exposure-normalized penalty and a Greek-ratio drift penalty. Empirical results on Nasdaq 100 equity options demonstrate that appropriately calibrated regularization simultaneously improves out-of-sample risk-adjusted performance relative to an unregularized baseline while reducing realized directional exposure.

articles.title: Hierarchical Multi-Task Learning with Liquidity-Aware Signals for Stock Forecasting
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Stock price forecasting is a long-standing challenge in computational finance, driven by the inherent randomness of markets and complex temporal patterns. While recent deep-learning models have raised forecasting accuracy by jointly modeling inter-stock and temporal price dynamics, they conflate inter-stock relationships with intra-stock temporal dependencies and focus solely on the univariate objective of price movement. To address these limitations, we propose LiMT, a Hierarchical Multi-Task Learning framework that integrates liquidity-aware signals for stock price forecasting. LiMT employs a Market Regime Encoder (MRE) module that first extracts contemporaneous cross-stock dependencies, then models each stock's temporal dynamics, yielding a unified latent state. Building on this latent state, we introduce a Liquidity-Driven Learning (LDL) module, a mixture-of-experts architecture that features cross-task gating mechanisms to jointly predict price movement, volatility, and trading volume. We further design an Adaptive Portfolio Optimization (APO) mechanism that converts multi-task forecasts into executable portfolio weights under transaction-cost and liquidity constraints. Extensive experiments on the CSI300 and CSI500 benchmarks show that LiMT performs best among strong neural and tree-based baselines across the reported metrics. In realistic CSI300 backtests, APO improves annualized return from 3.99% to 10.01% and Sharpe ratio from 1.22 to 1.86 over equal weighting, showing that the multi-task forecasts translate into deployable portfolio gains.

articles.title: OrderFusion+: Probabilistic Buy--Sell Price Trajectory Forecasting in Intraday Electricity Markets
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Intraday electricity markets enable participants to adjust energy positions close to delivery, with price forecasts necessary to support trading and the scheduling of flexible electricity resources as well as increasingly responsive consumers. Forecasting model specifications have progressed from using macro-features, such as renewable generation and load, to the micro-features of continuous orderbooks. A recent advanced deep learning model, OrderFusion, explicitly models micro-level buy-sell orderbook interactions. However, despite its superior comparative forecasting performance, it considers only one delivery product at a time, ignoring neighboring-product information. Moreover, when forecasting aggregated price indices such as the liquid German ID3, ID2, and ID1 products, it omits the information contained in price trajectories. In contrast, pretrained time-series foundation models have shown success in financial, renewable-energy, and day-ahead electricity price forecasting. However, their performance on intraday orderbook data remains an open research question of considerable practical importance. In this paper, we propose OrderFusion+, an open-source deep learning model that combines historical orders from the target and neighboring delivery products to forecast probabilistic buy-sell price trajectories. We benchmark OrderFusion+ against forecasting baselines and pretrained foundation models, and investigate dynamic market conditions through the designed dynamic masking mechanism, revealing insights into market efficiency. The implementation and forecasts can be found at: https://runyao-yu.com/OrderFusion/

articles.title: WaVeFuse: Regime-Adaptive Equity Index Forecasting via Channel-Wise Wavelet Denoising and Vertical Attention Fusion
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Hybrid Deep Learning for equity index forecasting is limited by three problems: propagation of OHLCV noise into derived technical indicators (TIs), channel-indiscriminate multi-scale decomposition that conflates heterogeneous frequency signatures, and static multi-branch fusion that cannot adapt to market regime shifts. WaVeFuse addresses these limitations through a unified dual-branch architecture. Symlet-4 wavelet denoising (level 2, MAD soft threshold) suppresses microstructure noise in OHLCV. Seven low-lag TIs computed from denoised prices are encoded by a causal channel-wise continuous wavelet transform (Morlet, 32 scales) into a per-timestep scale-space matrix. A CNN-BiLSTM branch captures temporal dynamics, while a dual-layer Transformer (heads=4, dk in {16, 32}) models inter-scale spectral dependencies, and their representations are integrated by a 2-token softmax gate Vertical Attention Fusion (VAF) that dynamically reweights branches as market regimes shift. Evaluated under walk-forward validation (WFV) on KOSPI, DAX, NYSE Composite, and Russell 2000 (2010-2023), WaVeFuse achieves R2 = 0.81-0.96 and directional accuracy 70.5-78.3%. It outperforms seven state-of-the-art models by 8.9-20.2% MAE across twelve dataset-period configurations. Diebold-Mariano statistics (4.62-10.38, p<0.001) confirm superiority over a well-tuned XGBoost benchmark across four indices. Ablation verifies component-wise contributions. Under realistic backtesting with 10 basis point transaction costs, WaVeFuse's directional strategy achieves a mean Sharpe ratio of 3.69 across four markets and limits maximum drawdown to 7.5% during the COVID-19 crash. With 152k parameters (0.68MB) and sub-1.3ms GPU inference, WaVeFuse delivers a computationally efficient, regime-robust framework suitable for research and decision-support deployment.

articles.title: OpenAI Targets Junior Banker Work With ChatGPT For Financial Services
articles.query: site:forbes.com ("generative AI" OR ChatGPT OR LLM) (finance OR bank OR investment OR insurance OR trading)
articles.text:
OpenAI has launched ChatGPT for Financial Services, an enterprise product developed with Morgan Stanley and Evercore, running on GPT-6 Astra. This specialized AI automates tasks traditionally performed by junior bankers, such as comparable-company analysis and pitchbook creation. A key feature is its native access to extensive financial data from sources like LSEG and PitchBook, providing auditable citations. While OpenAI frames it as a productivity tool, not a job replacement, industry experts express concerns about "cognitive atrophy" if AI handles reasoning crucial for learning. Labor data already shows a decline in employment for young workers in AI-exposed fields, driven by fewer new hires. This development raises significant questions about the future of junior banking roles, potentially shifting responsibilities to verifying AI output or leading to reduced hiring.
OpenAI on Thursday introduced ChatGPT for Financial Services , a version of its enterprise product built to research companies, analyze financial data and produce the client presentations that investment banks run on. The tasks it performs out of the box — comparable-company analysis, LBO modeling, buyer screening, earnings analysis, pitchbook preparation — are the tasks Wall Street has assigned to its youngest employees for decades.
The product is a tailored build of ChatGPT Work developed with Morgan Stanley and Evercore as design partners, according to Nick Turley, OpenAI’s vice president of product. It runs on GPT-6 Astra, the company’s newest model.
The distinction from the base enterprise product is data. ChatGPT for Financial Services ships with native access to financial statements, earnings transcripts, company fundamentals and private-company data from LSEG, Daloopa, PitchBook and Crunchbase , plus automated access to a firm’s existing data subscriptions.
Every figure carries a citation that traces back to the source filing, charts can be audited against the underlying numbers, and administrators get controls for sensitive deal materials.
In a live demonstration, Turley had the system evaluate a potential M&A target, pull the relevant figures and produce a formatted PowerPoint deck in the bank’s own template. The hard part, he told reporters, was not making slides that look good but making slides that make sense: the model had to select the right peer set, load prices into a spreadsheet, verify the chart against the data and explain a sell-off and rebound.
Turley said demand for the product was strong and that OpenAI plans similar sector-specific versions beyond finance. He declined to name any banks that have signed on.
The launch fits a pattern. OpenAI’s chief financial officer, Sarah Friar, told investors in August that the company’s enterprise business now generates more revenue than its consumer business. The company is widely expected to pursue an initial public offering, and finance is a market where its rivals arrived first: Anthropic released Claude for Financial Services last year.
Banks are among the highest-value customers in software. They pay for data, they pay for reliability, and they employ tens of thousands of people whose daily work maps closely to what large language models do well. That combination makes investment banking a natural first vertical — and a revealing one.
Asked by CNBC whether the product would reduce the need to hire junior bankers, Turley described it as a productivity tool rather than a replacement. Analysts work 100-hour weeks, he said, and the effect would resemble what Microsoft Excel did for the industry: faster, better analysis from the same people.
The comparison is worth examining, because the two technologies differ in one important respect. Excel executed the analyst’s reasoning faster. It did not choose the peer set, decide which chart mattered or explain the sell-off. A tool that performs those steps is doing the part of the job that trained the analyst in the first place.
That concern is not coming only from outside the industry. On an August 24 episode of Goldman Sachs’ Exchanges podcast , Chris Churchman — a partner who leads the bank’s Marquee platform and co-chairs its Global Banking and Markets AI working group — warned of what he called “cognitive atrophy” if bankers outsource their reasoning to models.
Much of the knowledge in finance is tacit and learned by doing, he said, and he compared the risk to the way GPS eroded people’s sense of direction. Goldman, he acknowledged, has not settled how much of that early-career work it will automate.
The apprenticeship question has a measurable early signal. Research from Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab , updated in August, finds that employment among workers aged 22 to 25 in the occupations most exposed to generative AI now sits 19% below where it would be had it tracked their less-exposed peers.
Experienced workers in the same occupations show no comparable gap. The researchers attribute the divergence to firms hiring fewer young workers, not to layoffs of those already employed, and they find the decline concentrated where AI use is automating rather than complementary.
The Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas reached a consistent conclusion in a January analysis : employment losses tied to AI exposure appear only among younger workers, and they are driven mainly by fewer people entering those occupations from outside the labor force.
Investment banking is a specific case within that broader pattern, and the pattern is what the OpenAI launch makes concrete. If a model can produce a defensible pitchbook in minutes, the economic logic of a two-year analyst program — in which a bank pays a recent graduate to learn by producing that same pitchbook slowly, under supervision — changes.
None of this means the analyst role disappears. It means the role’s content is up for redesign. The plausible future is one in which junior bankers spend less time assembling decks and more time verifying model output, pressure-testing assumptions and sitting in on the client conversations that used to be reserved for their seniors. Whether banks actually build that version of the job, or simply hire fewer people, is the decision that matters.
Seb Kirk, chief executive of the AI platform GaiaLens, put the stakes plainly in an interview with Moneywise : nobody learned judgment from reformatting a deck at 2 a.m., but handling the numbers yourself is how you noticed when one of them was wrong.
OpenAI has built a tool that handles the numbers. What the industry does with the people who used to is the story that will play out over the next hiring cycle.

articles.title: VertiFuseX: Generalizable Financial Forecasting via Multi-Stream Temporal Fusion
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Stock price prediction remains challenging due to the non-stationary and noisy nature of financial time series. Existing deep learning models often rely on rigid decision-level fusion, ad hoc hyperparameter tuning, and compressed final-layer outputs, causing information loss, overfitting, and limited cross-market generalization. We propose VertiFuseX, a hybrid LSTM architecture using penultimate-layer vertical fusion of multi-scale temporal representations. VertiFuseX stacks and reweights penultimate features from LSTM, Bi-LSTM, and St-LSTM branches, integrates a parallel DNN stream, and jointly optimizes all components via backpropagation under a fixed hyperparameter configuration. This preserves richer intermediate temporal information across scales. Evaluated on 15 years (2010-2024) of closing prices from 10 global equity indices using strict chronological out-of-sample testing with the final 365 trading days held out, VertiFuseX achieves 30-54% MAPE reductions and over 40% improvements in MAE and RMSE versus LSTM-based baselines, and outperforms seven state-of-the-art models across 33 metric-dataset comparisons. Ablation studies confirm penultimate-layer fusion drives these gains over final-layer fusion and decision-level ensembling. Gradient-based saliency analysis shows consistent emphasis on mid-range dependencies at lags 9-15 days. Economic validation via algorithmic trading simulation under extreme market regimes shows reduced maximum drawdowns and superior risk-adjusted returns. With 675k parameters, a 2.6 MB memory footprint, and 1.5 ms/sample inference latency, VertiFuseX offers a lightweight, interpretable, deployment-ready framework for robust financial forecasting.

articles.title: Deep Learning of Robust Market Making under Regime-Switching Order Flow
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Classical market-making strategies based on stochastic control, such as the Avellaneda--Stoikov and the Guéant--Lehalle--Fernandez-Tapia (GLFT) extension, provide closed-form quoting approximations, but rest on assumptions that break down at realistic microstructure timescales. One of them is that order flow is stationary, while empirical evidence points to the existence of regimes, possibly associated with algorithmic execution of metaorders. In our experiments, persistent directional flow makes stationary controllers unprofitable. In this paper, we develop a deep reinforcement-learning market maker (RLMM)---a Rainbow-style distributional deep Q-network which is calibrated and tested in a zero-intelligence limit order book. We find that, in the stationary setting, RLMM outperforms GLFT at comparable levels of profit and loss (PnL) dispersion. The stationarily trained RLMM is more robust to flow asymmetry than GLFT, but still suffers inventory saturation and large drawdowns under persistent directional flow. Training a separate RLMM under regime-switching flow, with a Bayesian flow-belief signal and a queue-adjusted quote exposure signal, restores positive mean PnL in our experiments. A final scenario-bandit step prioritizes low-return scenarios and improves performance under varying regime persistence and directional correlation.

articles.title: Explainable Deep Learning for Price-Trade Dynamics: From Black-Box Forecasts to Effective Parametric Models
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Understanding the joint dynamics of prices and trades is central to market microstructure, where returns and order flow interact through nonlinear and state-dependent mechanisms. Linear models are interpretable but may miss these effects, while deep neural networks improve forecasting at the cost of transparency. We use neural networks as tools for structural discovery rather than only for prediction. A deep feed-forward network is trained on high-frequency returns and signed volumes for large- and small-tick stocks and compared with a linear VAR benchmark. The neural network improves predictive performance, especially for returns, revealing nonlinear dependencies beyond the linear specification. Using Shapley-based explainability, we show that the dominant contributions are concentrated at the most recent lags. Model-implied responses are consistent with conditional averages reconstructed from the data. Unlike empirical averages, however, the neural-network decomposition isolates individual regressor contributions to the aggregate dependence. Lagged signed volume generates sign-preserving and saturating effects, consistent with nonlinear price impact and order-flow persistence. Lagged returns act as state variables: when the previous trade does not move the price, the model predicts continuation in the direction of past order flow, whereas non-zero returns generate attenuation or reversal. Building on these findings, we introduce a parsimonious SHAP-inspired nonlinear parametric model. It reproduces the main return-volume dependencies, outperforms the linear VAR benchmark, and achieves performance comparable to the neural network. A multi-lag extension captures residual longer-memory effects while preserving interpretability. Overall, explainability offers a route from black-box prediction to economically meaningful parametric models of price and trade dynamics.

articles.title: Tabular Deep Learning for Algorithmic Trading: Cross-Regime Bayesian Optimisation for Equity Signal Generation
articles.query: arxiv:all:"deep learning" AND (all:stock OR all:market) AND cat:q-fin.*
articles.text: Algorithmic trading now represents a market exceeding $20 billion, where even marginal gains in signal robustness can translate into economically significant returns. Existing evaluations of equity prediction models do not explicitly target regime robustness during hyperparameter selection. Five model classes are trained on daily observations from approximately 300 large-cap US equities over eleven years, with Bayesian optimisation configured to target trading performance across three statistically different market regimes. Regime-robust hyperparameter selection is associated with out-of-sample generalisation, as signal precision remains above the random baseline across all four quarters of the test period, and portfolio performance slowly degrades under simulated input noise before collapsing beyond a defined threshold. No individual tabular deep learning architecture outperforms gradient-boosted trees, but combining XGBoost and TabNet using rank aggregation produces a Hybrid ensemble with an annualised return of 51.26%, a Sharpe ratio of 2.44, and a statistically significant CAPM alpha of 0.423 (p = 0.011). A near-zero beta indicates this outperformance is driven by stock selection, not market exposure. Alternative data plays a secondary role once technical and fundamental features are accounted for, as well as contributing more strongly on the short side than the long, and varies by model class. An interactive application makes these results explorable in real time, with live data integration the remaining step toward practical deployment.

articles.title: The $35 Billion AI Trading Loss Exposes The Real Risk Of Leverage
articles.query: site:forbes.com "artificial intelligence" (trading OR "stock market" OR portfolio OR "hedge fund")
articles.text:
The Situational Awareness fund, led by Leopold Aschenbrenner, suffered a $35 billion AI trading loss, topping historical records. After gaining 439% by June, the fund plummeted 67% in July. This massive reversal stemmed from extreme concentration in AI stocks like Sandisk and Micron, coupled with up to 400% leverage. When these holdings fell sharply, margin calls forced the fund into distressed selling. Citadel capitalized, acquiring $16 billion in assets at discounts. The incident underscores how leverage can strip investors of control, forcing liquidation even if the long-term investment thesis remains sound, turning a successful strategy into a forced exit. This highlights the critical risk of financing structures dictating market decisions.
The $35 billion AI trading loss attached to Situational Awareness will get attention because of the number. According to the Financial Times, it now sits at the top of its table of major historical trading losses. I think the most useful part of the story is how it happened.
Leopold Aschenbrenner’s fund reportedly gained 439% from the start of 2026 through June. Then the portfolio fell 67% in July. Even after that collapse, it was still up around 80% for the year. This was not a manager who spent six months being wrong about artificial intelligence. It was a hugely successful trade that became very difficult to control once the market turned.
What matters to me is what happened next. I have always thought investors spend too much time asking who wants to buy and not enough time asking who must sell. By late July, Situational Awareness was no longer making decisions from the comfortable position of a long-term investor. Margin pressure was now a key factor in the decision-making process. Citadel was on the other side. The AI thesis may still prove right. That almost becomes secondary once the financing structure dictates when positions must be sold.
In 2024, Aschenbrenner, a former OpenAI researcher whose views on the development of artificial intelligence attracted considerable attention, launched Situational Awareness. Those views translated into extraordinary returns during the first half of this year.
By the end of June, that success had also changed the shape of the portfolio. Sandisk and Micron Technology reportedly represented more than half of the fund’s disclosed U.S. equity holdings. By July 30, Sandisk had fallen 43%, and Micron was down 24%.
I do not have a problem with concentration. Some of the best investors I know have made their best returns by putting meaningful capital behind the few situations where they had genuine conviction. But concentration behaves very differently when substantial leverage sits beside it.
Situational Awareness reportedly used leverage of as much as 400%. Once its AI-related holdings began falling quickly, the question changed. It was no longer simply whether Micron, Sandisk, or the broader AI infrastructure trade would be worth more in two years. The fund needed enough liquidity to get through the next few days. That is how a good long-term idea can still become a bad position.
A winning investment tends to get larger without anybody doing very much. The price rises, confidence rises with it, and a position that began as one idea among many starts to dominate the portfolio. Add borrowed money, and your tolerance for volatility shrinks just as your confidence is likely at its highest. Situational Awareness may eventually be proved right about AI. Its problem in July was that the structure gave it less time to wait.
Owning a stock outright gives an investor one thing that is often underestimated: time.
The stock can fall 30%, and you can decide whether the thesis has changed. You can hold it, reduce it, or, if you still believe the market is wrong, add to the position. You may still make a terrible decision, but it is still your decision.
Borrow heavily against the position and the calculation changes. A lender does not care that you think the stock will recover in six months. If collateral falls far enough, more capital has to appear now.
Reuters reported that Situational Awareness faced margin pressure during the July collapse and subsequently removed all leverage from the portfolio. Aschenbrenner told investors that the fund had come closer to permanent capital impairment than it considered acceptable.
AI did not suddenly stop existing in July. The long-term spending plans around computing, data centers, and infrastructure did not disappear because some related stocks fell sharply. What changed was the fund's ability to sit through the volatility.
I have seen the same mechanism, on a much smaller scale, throughout my career in special situations. A SpinCo gets distributed to shareholders who never wanted it. Funds sell because the company is too small, falls outside an index or no longer fits a mandate. They are not necessarily telling you anything about what the company is worth. They are telling you something about what they are allowed, or required, to own. Leverage can create an even more brutal version of that problem. The seller loses the luxury of waiting for value to be recognized.
Situational Awareness reportedly sold the bulk of roughly $16 billion of listed equity positions to Citadel as it dealt with margin calls. Reuters later reported that some of those positions were acquired at discounts of more than 10%.
Citadel did not need to have a perfect view on where every AI stock would trade next year. It knew it was dealing with a seller under pressure. One side needed liquidity. The other had it. At that point the buyer has the advantage.
When somebody must sell, the price can temporarily tell you more about the seller’s circumstances than the underlying asset. This is one of the reasons I have spent so much time looking at forced selling in spinoffs and other special situations. Markets normally do a reasonable job of finding prices. They can become much less efficient when one participant is operating under a constraint that the other is not.
The consequences spread beyond Situational Awareness. Reuters reported that Jane Street suffered roughly $15 billion in July hit tied partly to its investment in the fund and other technology positions. The Wall Street Journal reported that Jane Street's original investment of around $2.5 billion had grown to nearly $10 billion before the selloff.
Jane Street’s exposure had become substantial precisely because the investment had gone so well.
We tend to think that risk lives in the positions that are going wrong. Sometimes the position that needs the most scrutiny is the one that has made the most money. It quietly becomes larger, your confidence has been repeatedly rewarded, and the assumptions behind it start to feel less like assumptions.
I do not see the loss as proof that the AI boom is finished. AI remains a real technological and capital spending cycle. Situational Awareness could ultimately be right about much of what it believes. Some securities Citadel bought during the July liquidation may have been sold at attractive prices. The problem was that a long-term AI thesis ended up depending on short-term financing.
Position size matters because even strong conviction can be wrong. Liquidity matters because markets do not always allow you time to change your mind gracefully. Leverage matters because it can take the decision away from you completely.
